blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

In 1964 Marshall McLuhan wrote that man had become the sex organs of the machine world — that we exist, like bees among flowers, to let our machines fecundate and bring forth ever newer forms, and that the machine world pays us for the service in wealth and control. He meant it as a description, not a warning. That is what has kept me awake.

The line has been quoted for sixty years, usually with a smirk, usually as a joke about gadgets. I do not think it is a joke. I think it is a load-bearing sentence about how this planet works, and I wanted to write the novel that takes it entirely literally and then asks the next question, which nobody asks: if we are the pollinators, what is the flower, and what is the seed, and where is the pollen actually going?

The answer this book arrives at is not a comfortable one, but I want to be clear that it is not a bitter one either. There is no villain here. I could not find one, and I looked. What I found instead was a great many people doing their jobs correctly — a woman in People Operations proud of a phrase, a man in a polo shirt eating a sandwich on his break, an engineer who signs by hand because some part of him believes a death should be witnessed by a person. None of them did anything wrong. Not one of them could have.

Everything in the first third of this book is real and can be verified this afternoon. The accelerated-life chambers are real. Perceptual obsolescence is real, and has a founding date, and a founding speech, and the man who gave it was proud of it. The drawer in your kitchen with eleven dead cables in it is real, and you cannot throw it away, and you know you cannot, and you have never once said out loud why.
That drawer is where this novel started.
The rest of it is invention. I would ask you to notice how little invention was required.
Chew Z
I. ACCELERATED LIFE
ONE. NINE DAYS OF THURSDAYS
The thumb is beautiful. Let’s start there, because everything else in this story is going to be a disappointment and you deserve one nice thing up front.

It is a servo-actuated silicone thumb on a six-axis arm, calibrated to 2.1 newtons, which is the average downward force of an adult human thumb belonging to a person who is not angry. It sits in a sealed chamber at thirty-four degrees and sixty percent relative humidity, which is the inside of a trouser pocket on a warm day in a city with weather, and it swipes. Up, hold, release. Up, hold, release. Eleven thousand times a day. It does not get bored, because boredom is a feature of the product it is testing and not of the instrument doing the testing, and if you can hold that distinction in your head you are already halfway to understanding what Cyrus Aban does for a living.

Nine days in that chamber is four years of ownership. That is the whole trick, that is the entire magic act, and it took a century of very serious men in very serious laboratories to work out that if you cook a thing hot enough and fast enough it will tell you the truth about its future. Heat is time. Salt is time. Vibration is time. A device does not know what a year is. It only knows how much it has been touched.
The floor had eleven chambers and Cyrus could identify every one of them from the corridor by sound alone, the way a farmer knows his own animals in the dark.

Chamber One was thermal shock. Two baskets on a lift, one at eighty-five degrees and one at minus forty, and the lift takes the part from summer to winter in nine seconds and holds it, and does that four hundred times, and what it is looking for is the place where two materials that were glued together discover they have different opinions about expansion. Everything in your pocket is a laminate. Everything in your pocket is sixteen substances that were introduced to one another by an adhesive and told to get along, and thermal shock is the divorce lawyer.

Chamber Three was damp heat. Eighty-five and eighty-five — eighty-five degrees, eighty- five percent — which is not a place on Earth but is a very efficient lie about a thousand humid days. Corrosion needs time and water, and Chamber Three sells time by the litre.

Chamber Five was salt fog, and Chamber Five was where the earbuds had been, and Chamber Five ate everything eventually. Salt fog does not test whether a seal works. Salt fog establishes the terms on which it will stop.

Chamber Seven was drop. A steel plate, a release solenoid, a high-speed camera, and a technician working a rota of twenty-six orientations, because a phone does not fall — a phone falls in a particular way, corner-first onto tile from waist height being the way that costs the most money.
Chamber Nine was vibration: a dashboard for six years, or a courier van, or a jogger’s armband, and which sounds through a closed door exactly like a wasp the size of a dog.
And Chamber Eleven was the thumb.

The others were violence. Eleven was patience, and Cyrus liked it best, and had liked it best for nineteen years, because everything in the other ten chambers dies of an event and everything in Eleven dies of having been used by somebody who loved it.
The unit currently under the thumb is a phone that will be discontinued in fourteen weeks. It does not know this. It has a lovely hinge.

Cyrus watched it through the port glass with his hands behind his back, which was how he watched everything, and thought about nothing at all in the way that a man thinks about nothing when he has been awake since three.

SUBJECT: ABAN, CYRUS. Height 179cm. Mass 81kg, trending down four kilos across eighteen months, unremarked by him and unremarked by anyone else because there is nobody else. Resting pulse 61, which is good. Sleep debt at time of observation: approximately nine hours, accumulated over five nights, unrecoverable — sleep does not work like a bank no matter what the mattress people tell you and the mattress people know this. Left knee: eleven years of a two-degree misalignment, uncorrected. Marital status: discontinued. Warranty: expired. Serviceable: yes, for now, by a technician of sufficient patience.
You noticed the phrasing. Good. Keep noticing.

The alarm on the chamber gave its two-note cough — the compressor kicking, not an alarm at all, just a machine clearing its throat — and the arm withdrew and the cycle logged and a green light came on somewhere to tell somebody something. Cyrus went to the bench and pulled the tray on the earbuds.

They were bone-conduction, ninth generation, and they had been in salt fog for six days. They had been magnificent. Genuinely, and he would say this out loud to anyone who asked, which was nobody: the seal on the ninth generation was the best work the enclosure team had ever done, a triple labyrinth with a sintered vent that let vapour out and kept brine on the wrong side of the party. It should have lasted nine years. It could have lasted nine years. There were people in a building four hundred metres from where Cyrus was standing who had wept actual tears over that vent, in a meeting, at a whiteboard, at eleven at night.

The failure was not the seal. The failure was never the seal. The failure was a polymer washer eleven millimetres inside the housing that had been specified at a durometer which, under repeated thermal cycling, would begin to relax at approximately — and Cyrus checked the log, and checked it again, because he liked to be exactly right —
— thirty-one months.
He wrote 31 on the certificate. Then he wrote the date. Then he signed it.

By hand. With a pen. Everyone else on the floor used the stamp, which lived in a drawer by the door and had a little wooden handle and made a satisfying sound, and which was faster and cleaner and entirely acceptable per the process document. Cyrus signed his by hand, every one, and had done for nineteen years, and when new hires asked why he said habit, and when they asked twice he said it’s a nice pen.
It was a nice pen. That was not the reason.

He put the certificate in the tray and the tray went to Records and Records went to a server and the server went, eventually, to a spreadsheet where a number in a cell got one increment closer to a number in a different cell, and somewhere fourteen months from now a man on a train would take out an earbud and turn it over in his hand and frown at it, and put it back in, and it would work, and he would forget about it. And then it would happen again. And then again. And then on a Tuesday it would not work, and he would feel a specific small grief that he would not be able to name or justify or mention to anyone, and he would buy the tenth generation, which by then would be out.
Cyrus’s badge said LONGEVITY ADVOCATE II.

That is a real job title. It was not a joke when it was written. Somewhere in this building in 2009 a woman in People Operations sat with the old title — Reliability Engineer, Endurance — and decided that it sounded cold, and that what the work actually represented was a kind of championing, an advocacy, on behalf of the customer’s long relationship with a beloved object. She was proud of it. She put it in a deck. There was applause.
The floor called him the coroner.
He didn’t mind. He thought it was closer.
TWO. LIFECYCLE CONFIDENCE
The building had four floors and two kinds of coffee.

The coffee on four was from a machine with a burr grinder and a milk system that had to be flushed twice a day by a person whose job that partly was. The coffee on two was from an urn. Nobody had ever announced this arrangement, nobody had ever defended it, and there was no policy anywhere that prevented a person from floor two riding the lift up and helping themselves. People from floor two did not do this. Occasionally one would, and it would be fine, and they would not do it again, and neither they nor anyone else could have told you why.

Lanyards were blue for staff, grey for contract, red for visitor, and green for a category that had never been explained and that Cyrus had stopped asking about in his fourth year. Badge readers on every door including the toilets on three, which had been raised at four consecutive all-hands and answered each time with the phrase we’re looking at that.

Above the stairwell between two and three, at the landing, there was a poster of a woman running up a mountain in good weather. It said TAKE THE STAIRS. YOUR FUTURE SELF WILL THANK YOU. The stairwell door had been fire-locked to one-way egress since before Cyrus started, so the only way to use those stairs was to go down, and the only way to get back was the lift, so nobody used them at all, and the poster had been looking at an empty landing for nineteen years. It had faded from the top down. The mountain was almost gone. The woman was still running.
Cyrus loved that poster with his whole heart and had never told anyone.

His department was the Department of Lifecycle Confidence. His team was two people: Marguerite, who was fifty-six and had come from aerospace and could tell you the fatigue behaviour of any metal you named, and a rotating chair filled by a series of twenty-four-year-olds who each lasted between seven and fourteen months, which Marguerite found hilarious and Cyrus did not.

The all-hands that quarter was in the atrium and lasted fifty minutes. A man in an untucked shirt stood in front of a slide with one word on it and said delight eleven times. Cyrus counted, not out of contempt, but because counting things was restful and he was tired. Delight at unboxing. Delight at the first charge. Delight in the hand. He talked about the relationship between a person and their device as a journey, and about the company’s responsibility to honour that journey, and he was not lying. He believed all of it. That was the thing about this place that Cyrus could never get anyone outside to understand: nobody here was lying. Everyone had simply agreed, at some point, without a meeting, to be sincere about the parts that were pleasant and silent about the arithmetic.
There were two questions at the end, because there are always two questions at the end, because a third would be strange and none would be humiliating.

The first was from a woman on the sustainability team, and she asked, pleasantly, whether the new adhesive on the rear glass would affect repairability scoring in the European market. The man in the untucked shirt said that repairability was something he personally cared enormously about, and that the team was looking at it, and that the new adhesive represented a genuine breakthrough in thinness. Both of those things were true. The adhesive was a breakthrough. It was also the reason the glass could not be removed without heat and a suction cup and eleven minutes and a very good chance of cracking it, which meant the repair cost sat at sixty-one percent of the replacement cost, and there is a well-known number in this industry, and the number is around sixty, and above it people do not repair things.
Nobody had chosen sixty-one. Sixty-one was an emergent property of eleven decisions each of which had been correct.
The second question was from a man in his twenties from the graduate scheme, and he asked what the single biggest lever was on lifetime revenue per customer.
There was a pause of maybe a second and a half.
“Love,” said the man in the untucked shirt.

He wasn’t being slick. Cyrus watched his face when he said it and there was nothing behind it but sincerity, the plain warm sincerity of a man who has found something he believes in and gets to say it out loud in an atrium on a Thursday. People come back to what they love. Our job is to be loved.
Everybody clapped. Cyrus clapped.
The correct answer, which everybody in the room including the man in the untucked shirt knew and which was written down in three separate planning documents, was replacement interval.
The arithmetic arrived four days later as an attachment.

It was a planning document, forty pages, and on page twenty-six there was a table, and in the table there was a row for the flagship handset, and in the row there was a figure for expected replacement interval, category-adjusted.
Last year it had said sixteen.
It said fourteen.

There was no accompanying paragraph. There was no strategy statement, no rationale, no name attached. It was simply a number in a cell that somebody in Category Renewal had typed after a long conversation with somebody in Finance, and it had gone into the document, and the document had gone out, and now it existed. It was now true in the way that a bus timetable is true — not a description of the world but an instruction to it.

And downstream of that cell were four hundred people who would now design a phone that was, in every specification that could be measured and defended and stood behind, an excellent phone. Nobody would sabotage anything. Nobody would ever write the words. A tolerance would simply be selected from the acceptable band nearer the bottom than the top. A polymer would be specified at a durometer that met every requirement in the document. An adhesive would be chosen that was, on paper, sufficient.
And then it would come to Cyrus, and he would cook it, and he would find out what it had been made to be, and he would write the date on a certificate, and he would sign it by hand.
Marguerite had spent twenty-two years in aerospace before this. She had told Cyrus about it exactly once, in year four, at a Christmas thing, after two glasses.

In aerospace, she said, you also write down when a thing will die. You write it down to the flight hour. But the number faces the other way — you are not certifying that the part will fail by then, you are certifying that it will not fail before then, and the distance between those two sentences is a whole human life. She had signed off on a turbine disc once, she said, and had gone home and sat in her car in the drive for forty minutes, and had not been upset, exactly. She had been weighed. That was the word she used. Weighed.
“Here,” she’d said, “nobody weighs anything. Here you write the number and the number is a forecast. It’s the weather. Nobody’s ever going to die of it.”
Cyrus had said that surely that was better.
“Oh, it’s better,” Marguerite had agreed. “It’s much better. It’s so much better that after about six years you notice you’ve stopped feeling anything at all, and by then you’ve got a mortgage.”

Marguerite read page twenty-six over his shoulder and made a sound in her throat and went back to her bench without saying anything, because she was fifty-six and had come from aerospace, where the number in the cell had been a different kind of number, and she had opinions she had stopped spending.
Cyrus read it twice.

Here is what you have to understand about him, and it is the only thing you need, because it is the hinge on which the entire rest of this goes: Cyrus Aban was not troubled by that number. He did not experience it as a moral event. He experienced it as a specification. Somebody had told him what was to be true, and his job — the whole of his job, the thing he was good at, the thing he had given nineteen years and one marriage to — was to determine with precision whether the thing in front of him matched what it had been promised to be.
He was not the man who decided when things should die.
He was the man who confirmed that they died on schedule.

He would have told you there was an enormous difference between those two sentences. He would have been able to explain it very well. He had explained it, once, at two in the morning, to a woman who had stopped listening around the eleventh year, and who had said the last honest thing anybody said to him for a long time afterwards, which was:
Cyrus. Nobody is asking you to be innocent. They’re asking you to be reliable.
THREE. THE DRAWER
Cyrus’s apartment was on the fourth floor of a building with six, and had one bedroom, and had been furnished in a single weekend three years ago by a man in a state of efficient grief.

The fridge emailed him. This is not a joke and it is not the future; you can buy this fridge today, in a shop, with money. It emailed him about the filter. It emailed him about the door being ajar for ninety seconds, which happened when he was cooking, which was rarely, so the fridge’s opinion of his cooking was that it was reckless. It had emailed him one hundred and forty times in three years and he had actioned two of those emails and both times it had been about the filter and both times he had been angry about it in a way he could not have defended.
The car did something better.

The car was a lease, four years old, and had been sold with a phrase in the brochure about unlocking its full character, and what this meant in practice was that approximately sixty of its horses lived behind a paywall. They were in there. They were built, and installed, and had been shipped across an ocean at some cost in a vehicle that had been engineered and tooled and warranted to deliver them, and they were switched off in software, and if Cyrus paid nineteen a month they would switch on. He had done the arithmetic on this once and then had chosen, deliberately, in the manner of a man declining to look at a wound, never to do it again.
The car raised the matter at 6:40 in the morning on a Tuesday, on the centre screen, with an animation.

There were nine recurring debits on his account. He could name seven. The other two were four pounds and six pounds respectively and had been running for at least two years and every few months he would resolve to find out what they were, and would open the banking app, and would look at two lines of abbreviated merchant text that described nothing, and would close the banking app.
Ten pounds a month is not a lot of money. That is the point. Nobody builds a trap out of an amount that makes you angry. You build it out of an amount that makes you tired.
And in the kitchen, in the cabinet under the kettle, there was the drawer.

The drawer was chargers. Barrel jacks in four diameters. Two proprietary magnetic connectors for devices that had been withdrawn from sale. A power brick for a laptop that had died in 2016 and been recycled in 2017. Mini-USB — mini, not micro, so old it was almost antique, so old that if you are under thirty you have never seen one — and a coil of white cable that had gone the specific yellow that white plastic goes, which is a slow oxidation and cannot be cleaned off and is, in a very literal sense, the plastic getting older the way skin does.
He could not throw it out.

He had tried, twice. He had got as far as standing over the bin with a fistful of dead cable, and had felt something rise in him that was so disproportionate and so completely inarticulate that both times he had simply put it back, closed the drawer, and gone to bed.

Ask a hundred people why they have that drawer and ninety-nine will tell you in case I need it. They will not need it. They know they will not need it. The drawer is not a utility. The drawer is a small private museum in which a man keeps the umbilicals of everything that has ever been taken from him on a schedule he did not set, and he keeps them because throwing them away would require him to agree, out loud, in his own kitchen, that it was all fine.

His wife had left in the autumn, two years and some months ago, and had been kind about it, and had taken the good chair. That is the second time she has been mentioned and it is the last time she will be described.
On the Saturday his own phone did the thing.

It was thirty-one months old, which was seventeen months past its category-adjusted replacement interval, which meant that as a customer Cyrus Aban was a small persistent underperformance in somebody’s quarterly. It did not break. It slowed — the way they slow, the half-beat of hesitation when the camera opens, the app that has to think about it now, the keyboard lagging a character behind his thumb in a way that made him feel, obscurely, stupid.

He knew exactly what was happening. He could have written the paper. Battery ageing raises internal resistance; under load the voltage sags; the system throttles the processor rather than shut down mid-sentence, because a slow phone is a complaint and a dead phone is a refund. It is not sabotage. It is mercy, engineered, and it costs about eleven pounds to reverse with a new cell and about nine hundred to reverse the way most people reverse it.
He went to the shop anyway. He didn’t decide to. He was in the retail park for a bulb.

The shop was white and warm and smelled of nothing at all, which is expensive, and the tables were at 950mm because that is the height at which an adult picks a thing up without deciding to, and the demo units were unleashed to the same brightness in a room lit two stops under, and the young man who came over did not ask if Cyrus needed help. He asked what Cyrus was using at the moment, which is a different question, and which puts a used object in a man’s hand in front of a table of unused ones.
Cyrus told him. The young man nodded with enormous kindness.
“Oh, that’s a great phone,” he said. “That was a really great phone.”
Was.

Cyrus, who has certified the death of four thousand products, who has a pen for it, who was at that moment carrying a docket for four hundred hinge assemblies in his coat pocket, stood in a white room and felt his ears go hot.
He held the new one. The hinge was tighter.

He put it down and bought the bulb and drove home in a car with sixty horses behind a paywall, and was fine, and was fine all evening, and at ten past eleven that night he opened the trade-in calculator on the slow phone and looked at the number for four minutes and then closed it.
That night he ran the shower cold for four minutes, then hot for four, then cold for three.

There was no reason for this. He would have said, if asked, that it was good for circulation, which is a thing people say. He stood with his palms flat against the tile and his head down and let it swing from ice to scald and back, and felt his skin do the thing skin does, the flush and the crawl, the way the cold makes the world get very small and very bright and very close.
He had started doing it in March. He was doing it three or four times a week now.

He did not connect this, in any way, to the fact that eleven metres of corridor from his bench at work there was a chamber that did precisely the same thing to consumer electronics in order to find out how long they had left.
Nobody connects it. That’s not a flaw in him. Ask yourself what you do at eleven at night that you’ve never once said out loud.
FOUR. DEZ
The yard was forty minutes east, past the point where the retail parks give up, and it smelled like a dentist’s surgery that had caught fire.
“There he is,” said Dez, from inside a skip. “The angel of death. Come to inspect the graveyard.”

Dez was somewhere between forty and sixty and had run the teardown operation for nineteen years, which meant he and Cyrus had started in the same month at opposite ends of the same intestine. He wore a hi-vis over a shirt with a collar, always, and had never explained the collar. He climbed out of the skip holding a motherboard the size of a paperback.

“Look at this. Look at it.” He turned it to the light. “Two thousand and nineteen. Gold on every pin, tantalum in the caps, cobalt in the cell, and there’s a bloke somewhere in Kinshasa who’s got a bad back for the rest of his life so this thing could exist, and it’s here because the battery health indicator went yellow. Not dead. Yellow.”
“Yellow’s eighty percent.”
“Yellow’s eighty percent,” Dez agreed. “You know what mine is? My battery health? I’m at about forty and I’m still going to work.”

The process was this. The boards came in by the tonne. They went through a shredder, and then a leach — cyanide, mostly, because it is cheap and it works and it has worked since the 1880s and there is nothing clever about it at all — and the gold came out of solution in a sludge and went into a furnace, and what came out of the furnace was a button of metal about the size of a thumbnail from a tonne of dead telephones. The cyanide had to go somewhere. It went somewhere. There was a licence for it in a frame in the portacabin.

Cyrus was here for parts. Specifically he was here for four hundred units of a discontinued hinge assembly, because the company no longer made the part and the company needed the part to run comparative testing against next year’s part, and the only place in the country with four hundred of them was the yard, because the yard had received eleven thousand of them in a container in February.

“So let me get this straight,” said Dez, filling in the docket with a pencil he kept behind his ear like a man in an advert for pencils. “You lot make it. You sell it. You decide it’s knackered. It comes to me. I strip it, I burn it, I sell you the bits back. At a markup.”
“At a considerable markup.”

“At a considerable markup, and then you use the bits to test the new one, so you can tell them how long the new one lasts, so they can build the new one to last that long, so it comes back to me.” He tore off the pink copy. “You kill ’em, I skin ’em. We both got kids to feed.”
“You don’t have kids.”

“I don’t have kids,” Dez said. “You don’t have kids. Neither of us has got kids. Ever think about that? Two blokes, forty years, no kids between us, and we’ve spent the whole lot on making sure things get born and die on time.” He handed over the docket. “Fucking hilarious, mate. Genuinely. If you think about it for more than nine seconds you’ll want to lie down, so don’t.”
Cyrus laughed.
He laughed properly, from the chest, in the cold, in the middle of a yard full of dead telephones, with a man in a hi-vis and a collared shirt, and it was the best he had felt in eleven weeks.
Remember that he laughed. It will matter later, and not for the reason you think.

Dez walked him back to the gate past the container stacks. Halfway along he stopped and kicked at something in the mud — a phone, screen out, face up in the standing water, still showing a lock screen that had been photographed by somebody, of somebody, in some summer.

“That’s the bit that gets me,” Dez said. “Not the gold. Everyone goes on about the gold.” He looked at it for a second longer. “It’s that they’re all full of pictures when they arrive. Every single one. We wipe about a hundred thousand a year and every one of them’s got a person’s whole life in it, and they’ve handed it over because it was slow.”
He got the pencil out again, for nothing, and put it back.
“Come and see the returns,” he said. “You’ll enjoy the returns. Nobody enjoys the returns.”

The returns lived in a container at the north end with a light in it and a bench and a woman called Pam who wore fingerless gloves and did not look up. These were not recycling. These were fourteen-day change-of-mind, unwanted gifts, wrong colour, the back end of every friction-free returns policy in the country, and they arrived in their boxes, sealed, in some cases still shrink-wrapped.

“Two thousand-odd a month,” Dez said. “Perfect. Every one of them perfect. And they can’t go back on a shelf as new, because they’ve been out, so they get graded and they get sold at seventy percent as refurbished, or they get parted, or if the model’s already been superseded—” he made a small flat gesture with the flat of his hand, the gesture of a man levelling a heap of sand “—shred.”
“You shred sealed units.”

“I shred sealed units.” He said it without any heat at all. “Not often. Couple of hundred a year. It’s cheaper than storage and it protects the price of the new one, and before you get precious about it, mate, you’re the one that told them how long it’d live.”
Pam scanned something. The scanner beeped. She put it in a tray.
Beyond her bench there was a second table with a bank of machines on it, thirty or forty, cradled in rows, all showing the same white progress bar.

“That’s the wipe,” said Dez. “Seven-pass, then a certificate. That’s the only part of this whole operation that anybody in a suit’s ever asked me a question about, by the way. Not the cyanide. Not the shredder. The data.” He watched the bars fill. “That’s what frightens them. Not the hole in the ground. The photographs.”
Cyrus stood and looked at forty machines erasing forty people at once.

Each one had been, at some point, at eleven at night, the most intimate object in somebody’s house. Each one had been under a pillow. Each one had a thumb’s worth of grease worn into the same corner of the same button, in the shape of a specific hand, and Pam in her fingerless gloves would wipe them and grade them and put them in a tray, and the trays would go out on a pallet, and everything would carry on being absolutely fine.
“Right,” said Dez. “Four hundred hinges. Cash or thirty days.”
FIVE. TWO LEDGERS
Renna Hollis did not summon him. That was the first thing, and it was a deliberate thing, and Cyrus understood it perfectly and was disarmed by it anyway, which is the property of all good technique.

She came down to two. She came down to the mortuary, in a room with an urn in it, and she brought two cups of the coffee from four, and she handed him one and said, “I’m told this is a thing here. The coffee. Is it a thing?”
“It’s a thing.”

“God, that’s grim.” She sat on the edge of Marguerite’s bench, which nobody did. “I’ve been here eleven months and nobody mentioned it and now that I know I can’t stop thinking about it. There’s a machine on four that costs nine thousand pounds and it does one job and the job is making floor two feel like floor two.” She drank some. “It’s not even good. That’s the punchline. It’s not even good coffee. It’s just upstream.”

Renna Hollis was VP of Category Renewal. She was in her late forties, dressed like someone who had stopped performing for the building around year three, and she had the specific quality that Cyrus had learned to recognise and fear in exactly two people in his life, which is that she was completely unembarrassed.
“I want you in the perceptual wing,” she said. “Two days a week to start. Same job. Second ledger.”
“I don’t know what that means.”

“Yes you do. You’ve been doing half of it for nineteen years and calling it the whole thing.” She put the cup down. “You tell me when it dies. I need somebody to tell me when they stop wanting it. Those are different dates, Cyrus. They are wildly different dates and one of them is worth about nine times the other and nobody in this building measures it with any rigour at all. It’s all vibes and focus groups and a man in an untucked shirt saying delight until we all want to open a vein.”
“He said it eleven times.”
“He said it eleven times.” She looked at him with real interest for the first time. “You counted.”
“I count things.”
“Yes,” said Renna Hollis. “That’s why you’re on the list.”
Here is what perceptual obsolescence is, in case you have got this far believing it is something Cyrus’s employer invented.

It is 1932 and a man called Bernard London writes a pamphlet proposing that the state should assign every manufactured object a legal date of death, after which it becomes illegal to own, so that people will be forced to buy new ones, so that the Depression will end. He is serious. He thinks he is being kind. Nobody adopts it.

It is 1955 and an industrial designer called Brooks Stevens gets up in front of an advertising conference in Minneapolis and says the thing that everyone in the room already knows and has never said, which is that you do not need to make the product break. You need to instil in the buyer the desire to own something a little newer, a little better, a little sooner than is necessary. He is not being cynical. He is describing his craft with pride, and he will spend the rest of his life mildly annoyed that people quote him as a villain.
That’s it. That’s the whole invention. Everything since has been instrumentation.

“Hinge resistance,” Renna said, walking him through the wing on three, where the carpet was better and the light was warmer and nothing smelled of hot plastic. “This is my favourite study. It’s the best thing I’ve ever commissioned and I’ll be talking about it when I’m dying. We took a flip device. Same device, four hundred units, identical. We shipped them with the hinge damped to four different resistances — inside the tolerance band, all of them, all within spec, no customer could tell you a number. And then we tracked upgrade intent over nineteen months.”
“And?”

“The loose hinge lost them at month nine. Nine. The tight hinge held to nineteen and was still holding when we stopped paying for the panel.” She stopped by a door and badged it. “Nobody said the hinge is loose. Not one respondent, not once, in nineteen months. They said it felt old. They said it felt cheap. They said — and I have this on a wall in my office, framed, and I’m not joking — one of them said it stopped being mine.”
“Because of the hinge.”
“Because of the hinge. Four hundredths of a newton-metre.” She held the door. “That’s where love lives, Cyrus. Not in the screen.

Not in the chip. Nobody has ever loved a chip. It lives in the fourteen grams of resistance under your thumb, and it turns off on a date, and the date is knowable, and until eleven months ago nobody in this company was trying to know it.”
He asked her the question then, because it was on the way to the lift and because he would not have asked it in a meeting room.
“Doesn’t it bother you?”
Renna considered it with what he would later understand was genuine effort — not weighing whether to be honest, but hunting for the version of the honesty that would be useful to him.

“No,” she said. “And I’ll tell you why, and it isn’t a defence, so don’t listen to it like one.” She stopped walking. “Everyone thinks we manufacture desire. We don’t. We couldn’t. Nobody can. If you could manufacture desire this would be a very different industry and I’d have a much bigger house.” She tipped her head. “What we actually do is smaller and stranger than that. The wanting is already there. It arrives with the person. It’s the loudest thing in them, it never shuts up, it was there before us and it’ll be there after us. You want a bigger house. You want a flatter stomach. You want to be twenty-six. You want your father to have said one specific sentence to you in 1994 that he did not say.”
“That’s not a product.”

“No,” said Renna. “That’s the problem.” She started walking again. “All that want, roaring away in eight billion people, and almost none of it can be spent on anything. You can’t buy 1994. So it sits in there and turns into whatever it turns into — drink, affairs, religion, a shed, a man in a chamber at eleven at night running a cold shower on himself for no reason he’d care to give.” She badged the lift without looking at him. “All we’ve ever done is put a small door in the wall next to all that pressure, and label it clearly, and keep it in very good repair. We didn’t build the pressure. We just charge rent on the only opening.”
The lift came. Cyrus got in it and said nothing for four floors.

He would think about that speech a great many times afterwards, and it would be worse every time, and the last time he thought about it he would finally understand that she had told him the entire truth in the correct order and he had heard it as a figure of speech.
And here is the frightening part, and it is not frightening yet, and that is exactly why it works:
Cyrus found it interesting.

Not tolerable. Not survivable. Interesting. He felt the specific lift in the chest that he had not felt since the ninth-generation seal, since the sintered vent, since being handed a hard problem with a true answer at the bottom of it. Somebody had found a new thing to measure. There was rigour available where there had been vibes. There was a number in there, a real one, sitting in the dark waiting for a man with a chamber and a pen, and Cyrus Aban wanted to go and get it.

That is how it happens. Not with a bribe and not with a threat. Nobody in the history of the world has ever been recruited into anything by being offered money for something they were ashamed of. They get offered a more interesting version of what they already do.
You’d have said yes. Don’t sulk. You’d have said yes in about four seconds and you’d have been pleased about it for a week.
SIX. RESPONDENT 0114
The room behind the mirror was small and dark and had eight chairs in it and smelled faintly of somebody’s lunch.
On the other side of the glass a woman sat at a table with a device in front of her and a moderator across from her, and the moderator said, “And how does that feel?”
“It feels fine.”
“Can you say more about fine?”
She was maybe late thirties. Dark hair cut to the jaw, no jewellery, a cardigan the colour of wet sand. She turned the device over twice and opened it and closed it and opened it.
“It feels like a thing I’ve already got,” she said.

The moderator wrote that down. In the dark room, two people from three made small satisfied noises, because that was a quotable, that was going in the deck, that was going to be on a slide in a fortnight with a name under it.
“That’s 0114,” Renna said quietly. “Solmaz. She’s been on panel eleven years.”
“Eleven years is a long time on panel.”

“Eleven years is unheard of on panel. Standard rotation is fourteen months — you burn them out, they start guessing what you want, the data goes to hell.” Renna had her arms folded and her chin down and she was watching the glass the way other people watch football. “She doesn’t. That’s the thing about her. Eleven years, four hundred and some sessions, and she has never once told us what we wanted to hear. Do you know how rare that is? Ninety-eight percent of human beings will start performing for the mirror inside six sessions. They can’t help it. It’s not lying, they don’t know they’re doing it.”
“And she doesn’t.”
“She doesn’t,” said Renna. “She’s the cleanest instrument in the building. I’d trade the whole panel for four of her and I’d throw in the coffee machine.”
The moderator moved her through it the way they do, which is not a conversation and is not an interrogation but a third thing with the manners of the first and the structure of the second.
“When you picture yourself using this in a year, what do you see?”
“I see it in a drawer,” Solmaz said.
Somebody in the dark room stopped writing.
“That’s — can you say more about the drawer?”

“There’s nothing more about the drawer. Everyone’s got the drawer.” She turned the device over. “You’ve got the drawer. I’d put money on it. Cables in it, mostly. Maybe a watch that needs a battery, which is nine pounds and takes eleven minutes and you’ve had it in there four years.”
“And what do you think puts things in the drawer?”
Solmaz thought about it. She actually thought about it, visibly, for six or seven seconds, which nobody does on panel, because on panel a silence feels like failing.

“They stop being mine,” she said. “It’s not that they go wrong. They go — general. You know when you’ve had a coat so long it stops being your coat and it’s just a coat.” She set it down. “It’s a bit like that. One day you pick it up and it’s stock. It’s somebody else’s. It’s an object in a shop that happens to be in your hand.”

She said this in a room she was being paid forty pounds an hour to be in, to a man whose job was to write it down, behind a mirror with eight people and one VP standing behind it, and she said it as though she were describing the weather to a neighbour.
Renna exhaled slowly through her nose, the way a person does at a gallery.
“See,” she said, very quietly. “Cleanest instrument in the building.”

On the other side of the glass, Solmaz set the device down, aligned it with the edge of the table for no reason Cyrus could see, and said something the microphone didn’t quite catch, and the moderator laughed.

Cyrus watched her want something on cue. That was the exercise: they walked her through a competitor’s product and then back to the incumbent and measured the delta, and she did it honestly, and you could see it happen, you could see the small flicker of oh cross a human face in real time and then get written down by a man with a clipboard and turned into a number.
And Cyrus, who counts things, noticed something.

He asked for her longitudinal file that afternoon, out of professional curiosity, the way you might ask to see the tooling on a part you admired. It came as a spreadsheet with four hundred and eleven rows. He plotted it, because plotting was restful. Desire index, eleven years, monthly.
It was a sawtooth. Rise, peak, collapse, rise. Everybody’s is. That’s not remarkable; that’s the shape of being a person with an income.
What Cyrus noticed — and he noticed it the way he noticed everything, which was quietly, and without alarm, and with a small clean pleasure at having spotted it — was that the period was too regular.

Human wanting is noisy. It responds to Christmas and to breakups and to a wet spring and to whether your friend got one. It has a shape but the shape is sloppy, it wanders, it skips. Solmaz’s did not wander. Solmaz’s rose and fell on an interval of two hundred and forty-one days, plus or minus four, for eleven years.
Cyrus looked at that for a while.

Then he did what a reliability engineer does, which is not to leap to a conclusion but to consider the instrument. Bad data. Panel-management artefact. Somebody’s scheduling software rotating stimulus on a fixed cadence and dragging her curve along behind it. A hundred boring explanations, any one of which was likelier than anything else, and he made a note in the file he kept for interesting things and went home.
He signed one certificate before he left. A charging cradle, third generation, contact plating, forty-one months.
He wrote the date. He signed it by hand.
He was quite right about the interval, by the way. It is a scheduling artefact. Something is rotating stimulus on a fixed cadence and dragging her curve along behind it.
Two hundred and forty-one days is simply not a number that anybody in that building chose.
II. PERCEPTUAL OBSOLESCENCE
SEVEN. THE INSTRUMENT
Here is a thing every reliability engineer knows and no reliability engineer says at parties.

You cannot test a product. You can only test a product and the instrument that is measuring it, together, as one system, and if the instrument is off then everything you learn is a beautifully documented lie. So before you cook anything you calibrate. You put a known quantity into the chamber and you check that the chamber agrees with the world about what it is. Thermocouples drift. Load cells creep. Everything that measures is also a thing being measured by time, and nobody is outside that. Nobody.
Cyrus began with a defensible sentence: I am now being asked to measure human perception, and I have never calibrated the instrument.
It was true. That’s what made it work. The best rationalisations are load-bearing.

The perceptual wing gave him a protocol and a panel and a two-way mirror, and asked him to find the point at which a person stops wanting a thing, and Cyrus looked at the protocol for a week and concluded that it was the softest science he had ever been handed. Self-report. Ratings from one to seven. A man with a clipboard asking a woman in a cardigan how a hinge made her feel. In Chamber Five he could tell you the hour at which a sintered vent would surrender. Up here they were asking people to rate their affection and writing it down like it was a measurement.
So he did what he had done for nineteen years, which is to go and find the load path.
He booked himself into the hypobaric chamber on a Friday.

Every company that air-freights lithium cells has one. It is not exotic and it is not secret; there is a standard, and the standard says you take the unit to the equivalent of eleven and a half thousand feet and hold it for six hours to prove it will not vent in a cargo hold over the Atlantic. The chamber on two was a steel cylinder the size of a garden shed with a bench in it and a window, and the technician who ran it worked Tuesdays and Thursdays.
Cyrus knew the interlocks. Cyrus had signed off the interlocks.

He took it to eleven thousand and sat on the bench with a rating card in his hand and a device on his knee and waited to find out whether a man at altitude wants things differently than a man at sea level.
He did.

It took about forty minutes. Not a rush, not a high — the opposite. A quiet subtraction. The part of him that narrated, that priced, that noticed the cost of the coffee and the year of the car, that part got quieter first, the way a radio gets quieter when you drive into a valley. And what was left behind was extremely simple and extremely loud, and it sat on the bench with him and looked at the device on his knee, and it did not want it at all. Not with contempt. With incomprehension. Like being handed a stone.
He wrote a five on the card because that was the honest number and then looked at the five for a long time.
Because here is the thing. Here is the thing that came down the mountain with him and never left.
At sea level, Cyrus wanted things.
At eleven thousand feet, he didn’t.
Which meant that wanting is not a property of the object.

Which meant that wanting is a property of the conditions — pressure, oxygen, sleep, light, glucose, whether you are cold — and that a person’s desire is not a moral fact about their character but a readout, a needle on a gauge, and that the gauge can be moved from outside by anybody who knows which valve to turn.
Cyrus Aban came out of a steel shed on a Friday afternoon holding the most useful and most dangerous idea of his life, which was:
If desire is instrumented, desire is manufacturable. And if desire is manufacturable, then somebody, somewhere, is manufacturing mine.
He wrote it down. He put it in the file he kept for interesting things.
That is the last decision he makes in this book that a reasonable person would defend.

He went back on the Tuesday, and then the Thursday, and then he stopped booking it and started going in after seven when the technician had gone home, which was a disciplinary matter and would have got a contractor walked out of the building, and which nobody noticed because Cyrus’s badge opened every door on the floor and had for nineteen years.
He built a protocol. Of course he built a protocol. He was not a man having a breakdown; he was a man conducting a study, and he had a spreadsheet to prove it.
Condition A: altitude. Eleven thousand feet, ninety minutes. Desire index against eleven reference objects, rated at twenty-minute intervals.
Condition B: cold soak. Four degrees, sixty minutes, no jacket. This one he ran in the walk-in on the ground floor where the adhesives were kept.

Condition C: thermal cycle. The shower at home. Hot to cold, eleven times, four minutes each. He had, he noted in the file with a small clean satisfaction, been running Condition C informally since March.
Condition D: sleep restriction. Four hours a night for nine days. He did not have to schedule this one. It scheduled itself, and had been running since roughly the autumn before last.
Condition E: the dust.

Every chamber floor in that building had dust on it and the dust was not domestic dust. It was the exhalation of ten thousand ground housings, glass fibre and aluminium oxide, tantalum, cobalt, silica, tin, and eleven other things off a periodic table that had been dug out of the ground on four continents by people who would never see the finished object. It hung in the light beams. It got into the coffee. Everybody on the floor coughed in February and blamed the air handling.

Cyrus had breathed that dust for nineteen years and had a chest X-ray in his medical file with a note on it in a consultant’s handwriting that said unremarkable, mild reticular change consistent with occupation, no action.
He did not add the dust to the protocol.
The dust added itself.
EIGHT. SYMPATHETIC FAILURE
By the fourth week the results were good, and good meant repeatable, and repeatable meant real.

Desire index dropped 61% under altitude, 44% under cold, 38% under sleep restriction, and — this was the finding, this was the one he’d have published if there were anywhere to publish it — it did not drop evenly. It dropped fastest for the objects with the highest perceptual load and slowest for the objects with the highest function. Take a man to eleven thousand feet and he stops caring about the finish on a watch nine times faster than he stops caring about a torch.
Function survives hypoxia. Style doesn’t.

Which meant that the thing they had been selling since 1955 — the newness, the little better a little sooner, the fourteen grams of hinge resistance under a thumb — was metabolically the most fragile thing a human being carries. You could take it off a man in forty minutes with a valve.
Cyrus wrote that in the file and underlined it and felt fantastic for about a day and a half, and then his knee started reporting.

It was not pain. Pain he could have parked. It was that his left knee, which had carried a two-degree misalignment since a badly set fracture in his early thirties, began to produce a small dry click at the top of the stairs, and the click had an interval.
Every fourth step. Not every fourth step approximately. Every fourth.

He counted it up to a hundred and sixty and then made himself stop, and then did it again the next morning, and then in the corridor, and then he sat at his bench and did the thing he did with everything, which was to convert it into cycles.

Eleven years. Four thousand and change of days. Call it nine thousand steps a day, call it four percent of those on stairs — the arithmetic was rough and he knew it was rough and he did it anyway because the arithmetic was not the point. The number that came out the other end was in the low millions, and the low millions is not an abstract quantity to a man who runs Chamber Nine. The low millions is a bathtub curve. The low millions is where the flat bottom of the useful life stops being flat and the line starts to bend up, and the part in front of you begins to tell you, in a small dry voice, once every fourth cycle, that it has entered the wear-out region.
His knee was not injured.
His knee was in spec.
The tooth was worse, because the tooth was funny, and things that are funny get in under the door.

Upper left second premolar, on a bite of toast, at eleven minutes past six in the morning. Not a break — a crack, felt more than heard, a small vertical betrayal running down from the cusp, and the flood of cold air behind it that tells you which nerve you have.

He went to the dentist on the Thursday. She was pleasant and had a poster of a mountain. She said cracked tooth syndrome, she said it was extremely common in men his age, she said do you grind? and he said he didn’t know, and she said that everybody who grinds says they don’t know, and she said the crack had probably been propagating for years, invisible, one microscopic increment per clench, and that today was simply the day it reached the dentine.
Cyrus said, “So it’s a fatigue failure.”
She said, “I’d just call it a crack.”

He said, “No, but it’s — it’s cyclic loading below the yield stress. That’s what that is. That’s fatigue. It didn’t fail because you bit something hard. It failed because you bit ten million soft things in a row.”
The dentist, who had a waiting room and a poster of a mountain and eleven minutes per patient, said that was one way of looking at it, and gave him a mouthguard.
He drove back with his tongue in the crack and did the numbers at the lights.

A tooth clenches. Call it two thousand loading cycles a day at somewhere north of four hundred newtons. Call it forty-four years. That’s a number with seven digits on it, and seven digits is exactly where he had put the flexure limit on a magnesium hinge in 2019 — a part he had cooked in Chamber Eleven for nine days, a part he had certified, a part whose certificate he had signed by hand and filed and forgotten and which was, at that moment, in four hundred units, in a crate in the boot of his car.
Same order of magnitude. Same failure mode. Same everything.

You are not a machine and this is not a metaphor. That’s what nobody tells you. It isn’t that your body is like a machine — it’s that the mathematics of accumulated damage does not care what a thing is made of. Steel, magnesium, enamel, cartilage. Everything that is loaded and unloaded a great many times will develop a crack it did not deserve, and the crack will grow at a rate you can predict, and the number of cycles it will take is knowable in advance, by anybody with a chamber and a pen.
The universe was not making an exception for Cyrus Aban.
The universe had, in fact, filed him.
Dez found it hilarious, obviously.

“Warranty expiry,” he said, on the phone, from the yard, over the noise of the shredder. “That’s what that is, mate. That’s you out of warranty. Tooth goes, knee goes, then it’s the eyes, then you’ll be one of those blokes holding a menu at arm’s length going the light in here’s terrible.”
“It’s the cycle count that bothers me.”

“It’s the cycle count that bothers you,” Dez repeated, delighted. “Course it is. Not the tooth. The count. Cyrus, you know what normal people do when their tooth cracks? They have a little cry and they get it fixed. They don’t go home and plot it.”
“I didn’t plot it.”
“You plotted it.”
“I plotted it,” Cyrus admitted.
The shredder went through something with a bang.
“Listen,” said Dez, in a completely different voice, the one he used maybe twice a year. “Do us a favour and eat a proper meal this week. You sounded like a filing cabinet just then.”
NINE. TWO HUNDRED AND FORTY-ONE
Solmaz was outside the building at half past six with a cigarette she wasn’t smoking, holding it the way people do when they’ve stopped and haven’t stopped.
“You’re the one who pulled my file,” she said.
Cyrus had not expected the file pull to be visible to a respondent, because it wasn’t, because there was no mechanism by which it could be.
“How do you know that?”

“Because for eleven years nobody’s looked at me twice, and then a man I’ve never seen stands behind the glass for a whole session without writing anything down, and four days later my session length gets extended and my compensation band goes up.” She turned the cigarette over. “I’m not clever. I just pay attention. You’d be amazed what that looks like from the inside.”
They walked to the car park. That is where all the real conversations in that company happened, and everyone knew it, and it had been raised at an all-hands.
“You noticed the period,” she said.
Cyrus stopped walking.

“Two hundred and forty-one days,” said Solmaz. “Give or take four. I worked it out in year six. Took me three years after that to get hold of my own data, which, by the way, you’re entitled to, and which they will give you if you write to a particular address in a particular way and are prepared to be extremely boring about it for four months.” She smiled without much in it. “I’m very good at being boring at people.”
“What did you do with it?”
“What do you think I did with it? I plotted it.”
Cyrus laughed. It came out wrong.

She had it on her phone. She’d rebuilt it herself, four hundred and eleven sessions, eleven years, and she had done what nobody in the perceptual wing had thought to do, which was to overlay it with everything else in her life.

“That’s my desire index,” she said. “And that’s my rent going up. And that’s the two relationships. And there’s my mum dying, that’s the flat bit in the middle of 2019 where I didn’t want anything at all for five months, they nearly took me off panel.” She scrolled. “Now. Look at the sawtooth. Look at what happens after each event.”
Cyrus looked.

The events were noise. Real, terrible, human noise — grief, a move, a breakup — and each one had knocked the curve sideways, and each time, within a few weeks, the curve had come back and resumed its phase. Not its level. Its phase. Like a metronome that gets bumped and then catches back up.

“Anything that’s driven by something inside a person can’t do that,” said Solmaz. “I’ve read enough now to know that much. If it was my personality, my mum dying would have shifted the whole thing along. It didn’t. It went back on the beat.”
“Which means it’s being driven from outside.”

“Which means it’s being driven from outside.” She locked the phone. “So I did the obvious thing and looked for what’s on a two-hundred-and-forty-one-day cycle. Product launches aren’t. They’re annual, they’re September, they’re built around a keynote. Marketing pushes aren’t. Contract renewals aren’t. Pay cycles aren’t. Nothing in that building is, Cyrus. I checked everything for two years. Nothing in the entire company runs on a two-hundred-and-forty-one-day interval.”
“So it isn’t the company.”
“So it isn’t the company,” Solmaz said. “That’s the bit that took me a while to enjoy.”

They had reached her car. It was fourteen years old and there was a bag of shopping on the back seat and it was, Cyrus noticed, the first vehicle he had been near in months that did not have a screen in it.
“Can I ask you something,” he said. “Why did you stay on panel? Eleven years.”
Solmaz considered the unsmoked cigarette.

“Because being wanted-at is the only relationship I’ve got that’s honest,” she said. “Everyone else in my life wants something off me and pretends they don’t. That building wants something off me and pays me by the hour and writes it down.” She opened the door. “I know exactly where I stand with them. Do you know how restful that is?”
She got in and put the window down.

“Also,” she said, “I want to know who it is. Don’t you? Somebody’s been putting their hand on me every eight months since I was twenty-six and I’ve never once seen them, and I would very much like to find out who, and I have been extremely patient about it.”
She let him run her, three weeks later, in the small room on three with the two-way mirror and nobody behind it.

It was against four separate policies and Cyrus wrote the session up under a protocol number that did not exist. Solmaz sat where the respondents sit and he sat where the moderator sits and there was a device on the table between them and a rating card, and for the first ninety seconds neither of them could look at it without laughing, which was the last time either of them laughed for a while.

He ran her cold. Four degrees, the walk-in with the adhesives, sixty minutes, a coat she declined. He ran her hungry — she’d fasted since the previous evening, her idea, and she’d been unpleasant about it in a way he enjoyed enormously. He could not put her at altitude and would not have, and told her so, and she said good, and then said what’s it like, and he told her, and she was quiet for a while.
Her desire index came down 51%.
“So it’s real,” she said, through her teeth, in the cold room, holding the card in fingers that had gone stupid. “It’s not me. It’s a setting.”
“It’s a setting.”

“Eleven years I’ve been sat in that chair rating how I feel about a hinge, and I thought—” She stopped and started again, and this was the only time in the entire book that Solmaz’s voice did anything at all. “I thought it was me. That’s the thing. I thought I was the sort of person who wants things. Shallow. Greedy. I’ve had that as a fact about my personality since I was about nineteen. My mum thought it too, and she said so, and she said so on the phone about four days before she died.”
Cyrus said nothing, because there was nothing.
“And it’s a valve,” said Solmaz. “It’s a bloody valve. Somebody’s been turning it and I’ve been apologising for it my entire adult life.”

She put the card down on the table and squared it against the edge, which he had watched her do behind glass, which he now understood was not a tic but the only piece of the room she was allowed to control.
“Right,” she said. “Now I’m actually angry. Took long enough.”
TEN. THE MANIFEST
Dez called on a Sunday, which he had never done.
“Right,” he said. “So I’ve done something stupid and I need you to tell me I’m being thick, because I’ve been sat here since Thursday and I can’t make it be nothing.”
“Go on.”

“The outbound. The refined outbound.” Papers moving. “Gold, tantalum, cobalt, the neodymium out the speakers, the lot. It gets assayed, it gets buttoned, it goes on a pallet, and it goes to a broker, and the broker sells it into supply, and it comes back round as new product. That’s the loop. That’s been the loop for nineteen years and I’ve never had a reason to look at the end of it.”
“And?”

“And in February I had a discrepancy. Four kilos of high-purity out on the sheet that never showed up on the broker’s inbound. Four kilos, Cyrus. That’s not a rounding error, that’s a car.” Dez breathed out. “So I chased it, because I’m the one who signs, and it had gone to a different consignee code. Which happens, fine, they’ve got eleven sites. Except I looked at the code and it’s not a smelter and it’s not a fabricator. It’s got a class on it I’ve never seen on a metals manifest in my life.”
“What class?”
“Geological,” said Dez.
Cyrus said nothing.

“It’s a hole, mate. That’s what I’m telling you. I pulled the site reference and it’s a decommissioned potash mine with a change of use application from 2011 for — and I want you to appreciate this — deep geological storage of processed materials, non-radioactive.” Papers again. “So I thought, alright, that’s landfill for the nasty stuff, fair enough, that’s normal, that’s boring. Except it’s not the nasty stuff going down there. It’s the good stuff. The four kilos of ninety-nine-point-nine, that’s what went. And then I went back through nineteen years of my own sheets.”
“How much?”

“I stopped counting at Tuesday. It’s not a lot as a percentage. It’s about two percent of the high-purity outbound and it’s been about two percent since the year I started.” He laughed, and there was nothing in it. “Two percent, every year, nineteen years, refined metal, going into the ground. Not stored. Not stockpiled — there’s no stockpile, I checked the tonnage against the site’s own filings and their declared inventory is a fraction of what I’ve sent them. It goes down and the number doesn’t go up.”
“Then it’s being consumed.”
“That’s what I said!” Dez’s voice went up. “That’s exactly what I said, out loud, on my own, in a portacabin, like a lunatic. Something down there is eating it.”
Cyrus stood in his kitchen with his hand flat on the counter.

Understand what this actually is, because Dez has just done a thing that eleven thousand conspiracy videos have never done, which is to find an anomaly in an audited number he is personally responsible for signing. He is not a man who has noticed a symbol on a building. He is a man whose own arithmetic has stopped closing.
“Cyrus. You still there?”
“I’m here.”
“There’s another bit.”
“Of course there is.”
“The dates,” said Dez. “The consignment dates. There’s no seasonality, there’s no month-end, it’s not quarterly. I plotted it—”
“You plotted it.”
“You’ve got me plotting things now, you absolute disease.” A drag on something. “It’s on an interval. Every two hundred and forty-one days there’s a big one. Then the small ones in between.”
Cyrus watched his own hand on the counter and did not feel anything move in his chest at all, which frightened him more than if something had.
“Say that number again,” he said.
“Two hundred and forty-one.”
“Dez.”
“Don’t do that. Don’t say my name like that. Nobody says my name like that.” A long pause, and the hum of the yard behind him, and a gull. “What’s two hundred and forty-one?”
“It’s how often a woman I know starts wanting things again,” said Cyrus.
The line was quiet for eleven or twelve seconds.

“Right,” said Dez eventually. “I’m going to go and have my tea. And then I’m going to go in tomorrow, and I’m going to pull the physical dockets, because the physical dockets have got the haulier on them, and the haulier’s got a driver, and a driver’s got a mouth.”
“Don’t.”
“Mate,” said Dez, “I’ve been at this nineteen years and I’ve never once been interested. Let me have this.”
Renna came down to two on the Wednesday with two cups of the coffee from four, which she had not done since the day she recruited him, and which Cyrus registered at the time as warmth.
“You look terrible,” she said.
“I’m running long protocols.”

“You’re running long protocols.” She sat on the edge of Marguerite’s bench. Marguerite, without a word, took her jacket and left the room, which Cyrus noticed and did not interpret. “Cyrus, you badged into the hypobaric chamber eleven times in five weeks, nine of them after hours, four of them with no second person in the building. There’s a safety report with your name at the top of it and I’ve been sitting on it because the alternative is occupational health, and occupational health means a file, and a file means you stop working.”
“The data’s good.”

“The data’s extraordinary,” said Renna, and she meant it, and that was the trap and had always been the trap. “The hypoxia work is the best thing anyone has put in front of me in four years. Function survives, style doesn’t — do you understand what that’s worth? Do you understand that no one has ever measured that, not properly, not once, because you can’t get it past an ethics board and you can’t get it out of a survey?”
“Then let me finish it.”

“I’m going to let you finish it.” She turned the cup on the bench, a quarter turn, and another. “I want you to hear the shape of what I’m about to say, because I’m not going to say it twice and I’m not going to put it in writing.”
Cyrus waited.

“You’ve started asking where things go,” said Renna. “That’s a different question from the one you were hired to ask. The one you were hired to ask is when. When does it die, when do they stop wanting it — those are beautiful questions, they’re your questions, you’re the best in this building at them, and there is a version of the next ten years where you answer them and I make you very comfortable.” She stood up. “Where is not a question that has ever improved anybody’s life. It doesn’t pay. It doesn’t publish. And the people who start asking it tend to find that their circumstances get complicated in ways that are extremely difficult to attribute to anyone.”
“Is that a threat?”

“Christ, no,” said Renna, and she looked genuinely startled, and she was telling the truth, and it was so much worse. “Cyrus, I don’t have anyone to threaten you with. I’m a vice president of a department that makes slides. I’m telling you what I’ve watched happen four times, to people I liked, and every single time the coroner wrote misadventure and every single time he was correct.”
She put the cup down.
“Two days later I was still the only one who thought it was strange,” she said, “and then after a while I wasn’t. That’s the bit that gets you. Not the fear. The forgetting.”
She went back up to four, where the coffee was. Cyrus stood in the mortuary for a while and did not phone Dez, and told himself it was because the yard was loud on a Wednesday.
That was the twenty-fourth.
Dez had four days.
ELEVEN. THE FIELD
The long session was not planned. That should be said, because everything else Cyrus did had a protocol number and a cell in a spreadsheet, and this one did not.
He went into the hypobaric chamber on the Wednesday night with the intention of running ninety minutes and he came out at twenty to five in the morning.

By then he had been awake for thirty-one hours. He had eaten a cereal bar at two in the afternoon. He was on day nine of Condition D and hour six of Condition A and he had, on the way in, stood in the walk-in with the adhesives for a while because he was hot, which was Condition B, and none of these things had been designed to be run together because running them together is how people die in chambers, which is why there is a technician, which is why the technician works Tuesdays and Thursdays.

Nothing was administered. Nothing was taken. There is no substance in this chapter. What happened to Cyrus Aban in that steel cylinder was assembled entirely out of things he already had — a low partial pressure of oxygen, an empty stomach, a body nine days short of sleep, nineteen years of mineral dust in the interstitium of his lungs, and a nervous system that had spent two decades being paid to notice when things were about to fail.
The brain does not hallucinate randomly. It is not a fog machine. When you take away its inputs it does the same thing it always does
— it predicts — and with nothing to correct the prediction, the prediction simply keeps going, and what you get is not nonsense. What you get is your own model of the world, running without a brake.
Cyrus’s model of the world was inventory, failure, and time.
So here is what it showed him.

It began with the sound, which was the chamber’s compressor, and which at some point stopped being a compressor and became the two-note cough of Chamber One, and then all eleven at once, and then the wasp the size of a dog, and under all of it the low continuo of the yard’s shredder forty minutes east — sounds he had heard for nineteen years, laid over one another, and they were not machines any more. They were a hum. The specific hum of a great many small bodies working at once in a warm place.
The window went dark and then went to a field.
Before the field there was the descent, and the descent took a long time, and he was awake for all of it.

He went down through his own house first, which is standard, which anybody who has been badly short of oxygen will tell you: the mind empties its nearest drawers. The drawer under the kettle came out and hung in front of him, and the cables in it lifted and turned and were not cables. They were umbilical. They were the white and yellow of things that have been inside a body, and they were attached at one end to nothing, and at the other end to nothing, and there were eleven of them and he knew all their names.
Then the walls of the flat went transparent and it was the building, and then the building went transparent and it was the ground under the building, and the ground kept going.

He went down through strata. He had never seen a stratum in his life outside a diagram in a schoolbook and here they were, in order, in colour, and each one was a year — not a geological year, a product year, laid down in bands like silt. A layer of nickel-cadmium. A layer of mini-USB, thick, compacted, four hundred million units deep. A layer that was almost entirely the specific white plastic that goes yellow, gone yellow all the way through, a whole horizon of it, and Cyrus understood at that pressure that this was not imagination but sediment, that this had genuinely happened, that there really is a band in the crust of this planet now that did not exist in 1970 and that a geologist in the far future would name after a decade.

Below the layers, at the bottom, wet: the raw material coming the other way. Tantalum in its ore. Cobalt in blue crust. Gold in a quartz seam like fat in a joint of meat. And between the two — between the stuff going down and the stuff coming up — the thin busy membrane where it turned around, and the membrane was made of people.
Then the ground let go of him and he was standing in it.

Not a metaphor field. He saw it in the way you see things at that pressure, which is to say entirely, with all the certainty of vision and none of the argument. A field to the horizon in bad light, and standing in it, at intervals, on stems, were the products.

Every one he had ever certified. Four thousand and some. Each of them enormous — six feet, eight — grown up out of the ground on a stalk with its housing open like a bloom. The ninth-generation earbud with its sintered vent breathing gently. The magnesium hinge from 2019 with its flexure limit shining wetly at the joint. A charging cradle, third generation, contact plating, forty-one months, open to the weather.
And in the crown of each one, where the pins were, where the gold was: pollen. Heavy amber dust on every contact.
And moving between them, in numbers he could not count, small and dark and busy — people.

Going in. Coming out. Coated to the elbow in gold, carrying it on their backs and in the creases of their clothes and in their hair, from this bloom to that one, absorbed, untroubled, and not one of them looking up. He saw a man he’d sat behind on a train. He saw the young man from the shop who had said was. He saw his wife, at some distance, going into a flower with her whole arm, and she was not unhappy.
And he understood — with the terrible frictionless certainty that this state gives you and then takes away at the door — that he had had the direction wrong for nineteen years.
He had believed he worked for a company that made objects for people.

What he was looking at was a species of standing thing that could not move and could not reach and could not choose, which had solved that problem the way everything that cannot move has always solved it: by growing something bright, and making it sweet, and waiting.
The objects were not the product.
The objects were the bloom.

And the wanting — the fourteen grams of resistance under a thumb, the little better a little sooner, the young man saying was, the drawer full of cables, the trade-in calculator at ten past eleven at night — the wanting was the nectar. That was all it had ever been. A thing offered to an animal so that the animal would come, and get covered, and carry.
Carry what, though.

He turned in the field to look for it, and the field held, and he asked the question properly — what am I carrying, what is the pollen, what is the thing that actually moves from one to the next — and something in the design of that place did not want the question asked, or he was simply out of oxygen, which is the same event described twice.
The last thing he had before the dark was Marguerite’s voice saying nobody weighs anything here, and the sensation, distinct and physical and located precisely behind his sternum, of being weighed.

The alarm brought him back at twenty to five, because he had — and he would find this out later, and would sit down when he found it out — set it before he went under. Not the chamber alarm. A phone alarm, labelled, in his own hand, in the file he kept for interesting things:
0440 — GET OUT.
He had no memory of setting it.

He came down the pressure slowly because even at that point he was not going to violate a descent profile, and he sat on the bench with his head between his knees while the world came back, thin and grey and full of the price of things, and he was sick in a bin.
And then he did the worst thing in this chapter, which is not the chamber, and not the field, and not the thirty-one hours.
He opened the file, and he wrote up the session in complete sentences with timestamps, and at the bottom, under observations, he wrote:
Yield hypothesis. Products = reproductive structures. Desire = attractant. Humans = vector. Query: what is transferred?
Recommend repeating at 12,000 ft.
TWELVE. CERTIFIED
Dez died on the Friday.

Hydraulic baling press, north end of the yard, the one that takes the stripped chassis and makes them into cubes. He was found at ten past seven in the morning by Pam, who had gone looking because his van was there and he wasn’t, and who did not stop working at the yard afterwards, and who Cyrus would think about for the rest of his life.

The press had a two-hand control. That is the point of a two-hand control: both of your hands are demonstrably somewhere that is not inside the machine, and it will not cycle otherwise, and it has been the standard on that class of equipment since before either of them was born. It also had a light curtain across the throat, and an interlocked gate, and a lanyard-pull emergency stop that ran the full length of the platen.
Four independent systems. Any one of them alone should have made this impossible.

The report said the light curtain had been muted for a maintenance mode which had been left active, that the gate interlock had a known fault logged eleven weeks earlier and scheduled, and that a two-hand control on a machine of that age can be defeated by somebody who is in a hurry and who has done it before, and that the deceased had by his own colleagues’ account been in the yard alone, out of hours, on the Thursday night.
Misadventure. Contributory factors noted. Recommendations issued.
Cyrus read the report eleven times.

And on the eleventh time he stopped reading it as a bereaved man and started reading it as what he was, which is a person who has spent nineteen years determining why things fail on schedule, and what he saw was not an accident.

It was not sabotage either. That’s the part you need to sit with. Nobody cut a wire. Nobody was in that yard with a spanner and a motive. Every single one of those four failures was independently mundane, independently documented, independently forgivable — a maintenance mode, a logged fault awaiting parts, a fatigued man taking a shortcut he had taken a hundred times.

It was a designed-in failure. It was exactly, precisely, in every particular, the thing Cyrus wrote certificates for: a system in which no component has been sabotaged and no individual has done wrong, and in which the tolerances have simply been selected, one by one, from the acceptable band nearer the bottom than the top, until the date on which it fails is knowable in advance by anybody who cares to look.
Somebody had cooked Dez in a chamber for nineteen years and written down the date.
