At the funeral there were forty people and Pam sat at the back. Somebody had put a photograph on a board of Dez in the hi-vis over the collared shirt, holding a motherboard up to the light, laughing at something outside the frame.

There was a woman there in her sixties who turned out to be his sister, and who said to Cyrus in the car park, without any preamble at all, “He talked about you. He said there was a bloke at the manufacturer who was the only one who’d ever asked him a question.”
Cyrus said that Dez had asked him rather more questions than the other way round.
“Well,” she said, “he wouldn’t have told you that.”

Afterwards Cyrus went back to the yard, because nobody had told him not to and because the gate code was the same as it had been for nineteen years. Pam was there in her fingerless gloves, at the bench, working, because the containers still came.
“They’ve put a temp in the portacabin,” she said. “Twenty-six. Very nice. Doesn’t know where anything is.”
“Pam. The dockets. The physical ones, the paper. Did he pull them?”
She scanned something. The scanner beeped. She put it in a tray.

“Thursday,” she said. “He was in the archive container Thursday afternoon, three hours, and he came out with a lever-arch file and he was happy. I said what’ve you got there and he said—” She stopped scanning. “He said, I’ve got a name, Pam.”
“Where’s the file?”
Pam looked at him for the first time.

“There isn’t one,” she said. “There’s no lever-arch file in that portacabin and there’s no lever-arch file in his van and there’s no lever-arch file in his house, because his sister looked, because I asked her to. And before you say it — no, nobody came. There’s four cameras on that gate and I’ve watched all four, all night, twice. Nobody came in. Nobody went out.” She picked up the scanner again. “He put it somewhere. That’s all that happened. He put it somewhere on the Thursday and then on the Thursday night he went and did a stupid thing with the press, and both of those are true, and I’ve stopped trying to make them one thing.”

Cyrus drove home the long way and thought about how a system that has been designed properly never requires anybody to do anything. That’s the whole art of it. A well-made mechanism does not need an assassin any more than a well-made phone needs a hammer. You select the tolerances, and you wait, and the outcome arrives on schedule looking exactly like bad luck.
He told Solmaz on the phone that night. She was quiet for a while.
“Two hundred and forty-one days,” she said. “When’s the next one?”
He’d already worked it out. He’d worked it out in the car.
“Eleven days.”
“Right,” said Solmaz. “Then that’s when we go down.”
Cyrus went home and did not go into work on the Monday.

On the Tuesday he went in at four in the morning, badged through every door on the floor with a credential nobody had ever audited, and pulled the consignment records for a decommissioned potash mine with a change of use application from 2011.
The site had a personnel access provision. Of course it did. Somebody has to mop.

And Cyrus Aban’s badge, which had opened every door in that building for nineteen years, which had been issued to a Longevity Advocate II by a woman in People Operations who had been proud of the title —
— was already on the list.
It had been on the list since 2011.
III. YIELD
THIRTEEN. PERSONNEL ACCESS PROVISION
The mine was in a flat county four hours north and it did not look like anything.

That is the first thing and it is the worst thing and everything else in this part of the book rests on it. There was a road off a road. There was a hedge that had been maintained. There was a sign, brown and green, of the kind that local authorities put on light industrial units, and the sign said the name of a holdings company and underneath it in smaller letters MATERIALS RECOVERY — DEEP STORAGE, and there was a barrier, and beside the barrier was a card reader of the same make as the one on the toilets on floor three.
Cyrus badged it. It went green. The barrier lifted.
“That’s it,” said Solmaz. “That’s the whole thing? Nineteen years and it’s a barrier?”
“It’s a barrier.”
“I’d have felt better if it had been guarded.”
“So would I.”
There was a car park with nine cars in it, and lines painted, and two of the spaces were marked with a wheelchair symbol, and one was marked VISITOR, and there was a bin.

The reception was a portacabin with a laminated sign taped to the inside of the glass that said ALL VISITORS MUST SIGN IN and a book, and the book had been signed in by fourteen people that day, and the last entry was at 11:20 and said contractor — lift inspection.
Nobody was behind the desk.
Somewhere down a corridor a kettle came to the boil and clicked off.

The shaft head was a shed, and the cage was a cage, and it was thirty-one seconds down and there was a laminated notice inside it about capacity and a smaller laminated notice about not eating in the cage.

The temperature came up as they went. Potash mines are warm. Everything is warm at depth; the planet is warm, it has been warm since it made itself, and if you go down far enough into any part of it you are going into something with a body temperature.
The cage stopped. The gate opened.

And Cyrus Aban stepped out into a corridor with a floor of sealed grey epoxy, painted with a yellow walkway line down the middle and a chevron hatch at the junction, and directional signage in white on green — LEVEL 2 · RACKS A–M · WELFARE · ASSEMBLY POINT 4 — and a fire extinguisher on a bracket with an inspection tag hanging off it, initialled, dated eleven weeks ago.
There was a laminated evacuation map at eye height with a red YOU ARE HERE sticker slightly off-centre, as though it had been reapplied.
There was a vending machine.
It was lit. It was three-quarters full. Row F had sold out of one particular brand of crisp and there was a small handwritten note taped to the glass that said F3 STICKING — ENG AWARE.
“Oh,” said Solmaz, very quietly. “Oh, I don’t like this at all.”
“Say why.”
“Because somebody’s complained about the crisps,” she said. “Because that means there’s a somebody, and the somebody comes here every day, and the somebody’s biggest problem is row F.”
Cyrus looked at the note for a long time.

Every horror you have ever been sold has been dressed. It has had a lighting scheme. It has had a locked door and a keypad and a man with a clipboard who does not want you in there, because the drama of a hidden thing is in the hiding, and hiding is a promise: somebody knew this was wrong, and made an effort, and the effort is a kind of respect.

Nothing here was hidden. There was signage. There was a rota. There was a health and safety poster about manual handling with a cartoon man on it lifting with his knees. There was a first-aid box, and a defibrillator in a green cabinet, and a printed sheet by the lift that said THIS MONTH’S NEAR-MISS FIGURE: 3 with a little smiley face drawn on it in biro.
Somebody’s job was to mop this floor.
Somebody’s job was to draw the smiley face.
“Come on,” said Cyrus.
They followed the yellow line, and forty metres along it the yellow line went past an open door with WELFARE on it in white on green, and Cyrus, who should not have looked, looked.
It was a staff room.

Kitchen units along one wall in a laminate that had been fashionable in about 2004. A microwave with a splash of something orange dried on the inside of the door. A kettle. A noticeboard with a curling rota on it, and a fire-warden list, and a card that had been signed by eleven people for somebody called Deborah with 60!! on the front, and a takeaway menu, and a printout of a cartoon about Mondays.
Four chairs round a table. On the table, a puzzle book, open, with a biro in the fold.
A man in his fifties sat at the far end in a polo shirt with a small embroidered logo, eating a sandwich out of a plastic wedge and looking at his phone.
He glanced up.
“Alright,” he said.
“Alright,” said Cyrus.
The man went back to his phone.

That was it. That was the entire exchange. Two men said alright to each other in a kitchen, and one of them went back to a sandwich, and forty metres away and one level down there were forty thousand people in racks, and the man in the polo shirt would clock off at half five and drive home and probably think about the traffic.
Solmaz got them out of there and into the corridor and stood with her back against the wall.
“He said alright,” she said.
“I know.”
“He said alright and then he looked at his phone. Cyrus, he looked at his phone.”
“I know.”

“What’s on his phone?” She was not asking rhetorically. She had gone somewhere very cold and very precise. “That’s what I want to know now. That’s the only thing I want to know. What is that man looking at, down here, on his break, in the middle of all this. Is it football? Is it the news? Has he got a shopping app open? Is he choosing a fridge?”
Cyrus did not have an answer then.

He would have one in about an hour, and it would be worse than anything she was imagining, because the answer is that it does not matter what is on the phone. The phone is not the point. The man is not a monster and he is not a collaborator and he is not brave and he is not stupid. He is a man with a mortgage doing a shift in a facility, the way people have always done shifts in facilities — the way somebody drove the trains, the way somebody counted the inventory, the way somebody sat in a hut with a ledger at the edge of every atrocity that has ever been organised properly — and the reason it works, the reason it has always worked, is that at no point in his day is he ever required to look at the whole thing at once.
Nobody is. That’s the design. That’s what a system is.
FOURTEEN. RACKS A–M
You could hear it before you got there.

Not machinery. He had spent nineteen years learning machinery by ear and this was not it. It was low and wide and slightly wet and it had no rhythm at all, and it took Cyrus about four steps into the transition corridor to identify it, and when he did he stopped walking and put his hand out to the wall.
It was breathing.

Not one thing breathing. Not two hundred. A quantity of breathing, a mass of it, tens of thousands of chests going up and down slightly out of phase with one another so that the sound never resolved into a beat — it just went on, arriving and arriving, the way rain does, the way applause does when it has gone on too long.
Under it, felt more than heard, the hum of extraction.
And over both, from a speaker somewhere in the roof, at conversational volume, a calm recorded voice saying: “Rack C, tier four, intake complete. Rack C, tier five, commencing.”
Speaking to nobody. Announcing it to an empty corridor with a yellow line on the floor.
The doors were double, with a push bar, and a small square window at head height, and a sign that said HEARING
PROTECTION NOT REQUIRED IN THIS AREA.
Cyrus pushed the bar.

The smell arrived before the sight did, because he had his eyes half-shut, and it was not what he had braced for. It was not chemical and it was not death. It was warm saline, and scalp — the specific oily-sweet human smell of a scalp that has not been washed but has been kept at blood heat — and under that, faintly, the note that skin gets when it has been wet too long, that soft sour edge, the smell of a plaster taken off after four days.
It smelled like a very large room full of people sleeping.
Then he opened his eyes.

Twelve tiers. He counted, because he counts. Twelve tiers of clear-walled cells running away from him in a straight line under strip lighting to a point where the perspective closed and there was nothing but a haze of light and vapour and the suggestion of more, and then the row beside it doing the same thing, and the row beside that, and he turned his head and the rows went out to the left as well and he could not see the end of them in either direction.

It was not a cathedral. He had come down here braced for a cathedral, and there was a part of him that had wanted one — black chrome and a red glow and something to be awed by, because awe is survivable.

It was a shed. It was an enormous, well-run, brightly lit agricultural shed with a good extraction system and a mopped floor, and the aisles were exactly wide enough for the maintenance gantry, and there were number decals on every rack upright at two-metre intervals, and a spill kit mounted at the end of each row.
And in the cells, in the racks, twelve high, going away in both directions until the light gave out, were people.

They were not in fluid, which he had also braced for. They were on gel — a translucent support surface that took the body’s shape, the way a hospital mattress does for someone who will never move again, because that is exactly what it was and exactly who they were.
They were naked and they were clean and they were slightly wet.
Their eyes were shut. Most of them. Not all.
The first one Cyrus looked at properly was a man of about fifty in tier three, and Cyrus looked at him because he was directly at eye level and because his face was moving.

Not much. A flicker at the corner of the mouth. A tightening across the brow, held for a second and a half, released. The tiny involuntary lift at the outer eye that a human face does when it is surprised by something mildly pleasant. Then the brow again. Then, at the jaw, a clench — and Cyrus, who now knew a great deal about clenching, watched a man in a box grind his teeth at something happening behind his eyes and felt the crack in his own premolar like a wire.
He was not unconscious. That was the thing. That was the whole thing.
He was occupied.
The head end was the part Cyrus had been avoiding with his eyes and he made himself go there last.

There was no helmet. He had expected a helmet; everyone expects a helmet, because a helmet is a thing that comes off. What there was instead, at the base of the skull where it meets the neck, was a fitting — a low grey collar about the size of a bottle cap, sitting flush, with the hair grown around it and through it and, in the older ones, entirely over it, so that on the woman in tier nine you could not have found it at all without knowing.
Around it the skin had done what skin does around a permanent implant, which is to give up and make a seal, and the seal was pink and slightly raised and perfectly healthy.

It was not plugged into anything. There was no cable. There was a small dull contact face and a maintenance QR sticker on the cell wall beside it, and eleven inches away on the rack upright there was a mount, and that was all, and Cyrus understood with a lurch that the mount was for the reader, and the reader was on the gantry, and the gantry came round.
The gantry came round the way a milking parlour comes round.

The tube in his arm and the tube in his groin and the tube at his throat were not the horror. Cyrus made himself look at all three, one after another, and catalogued them like a man reading a bill of materials: feed, drain, airway. Fine. Understandable. Hospitals do this. He had an aunt who had been on less than this for eleven months and there had been flowers.
The horror was the face.
The horror was forty thousand faces, in twelve tiers, in a shed, all doing very small things, all at slightly different times, all reacting to something none of them could see.
Solmaz had gone about nine feet along the aisle and stopped.
“Cyrus,” she said.
“Yeah.”
“They’re not asleep.”
“I know.”
“No, but—” Her voice was doing something. “Cyrus, they’re not asleep. This one’s — look at her. Look at her hands.”
He came and looked.
The woman in tier two had her hands slightly raised off the gel, fingers curled, thumbs moving.
Up. Hold. Release.
Up. Hold. Release.

Eleven thousand times a day, in the dark, at thirty-four degrees and sixty percent relative humidity, at 2.1 newtons of downward force, which is the average force of an adult human thumb belonging to a person who is not angry.

Cyrus Aban stood in the aisle of Rack B and watched a woman he had never met scroll something that did not exist, and understood that he had been looking at the instrument his entire life and had believed it was the test.
There was a monitor at the end of the tier, on a swing arm, the kind that fitters use.

He should not have woken it. It woke to a touch, because everything does, because whoever specified it had bought the cheapest industrial panel on the market and the cheapest industrial panel on the market wakes to a touch.

And under that, a live feed, which was not video, because there was nothing to film. It was a text log. A plain scrolling text log in a monospaced font, the way a machine writes down what it is doing, and what it was doing was writing down her life.

06:41 — wakes. Ambient 19C. Partner absent (business travel, day 3 of 5). 06:44 — checks handset. 2 notifications. Affect: flat. 06:52 — shower. Water pressure nominal. 07:31 — commute. Delay 11 min. Affect: irritation, low. 08:02 — coffee, purchased. Cup: new supplier livery. Affect: mild positive, unattributed.
Cyrus read four hundred lines of it standing in an aisle.

It was so boring. That was what he could not get past. It was the most boring document he had ever read and it went on for six thousand two hundred and eight sessions and every line of it was somebody’s actual Tuesday.
And then, every so often, a line came through in a different colour.

11:19 — passes retail display. Observes handset, competitor, unfamiliar hinge geometry. 11:19 — DELTA. Preference expressed against unmodelled attribute. Vector logged. 11:19 — subject does not enter store. Subject continues to work.

Three lines. A woman in a rack in a shed under a field, who had not stood up since 2019, walking past a shop window that did not exist, in a city that did not exist, and wanting — for eleven seconds, for no reason, against nothing she had been shown before — a different hinge.
VECTOR LOGGED.
And then, four lines later, back to the commute, and the flat affect, and the water pressure nominal.
“What is it?” said Solmaz.
“It’s her day,” said Cyrus.
“What’s the coloured bit?”
Cyrus looked at three lines of monospaced text on a cheap panel on a swing arm.
“It’s the only bit they want,” he said.
The gantry came round at twenty past.

They heard it before they saw it — a soft electric hum on a rail overhead, unhurried, travelling, and Cyrus pulled Solmaz back against the rack upright out of an instinct that turned out to be entirely unnecessary, because the gantry did not care about them and would not have cared if they had been standing in the aisle holding hands.

It was a maintenance arm on a carriage. It looked like nothing. It looked like the arm in Chamber Eleven, and Cyrus, whose entire nervous system had been trained on that exact silhouette for nineteen years, felt his whole body go to attention as though somebody had called his name.
It stopped at tier three. It extended. It set a reader against the grey collar at the base of a fifty-year-old man’s skull, and it held there for four seconds.
There was a sound. It was very small.
It was the sound a card reader makes when it goes green.

Then the arm withdrew, and the carriage moved on eleven inches, and did the next one, and the next, and the next, down the row, at the pace of a man walking slowly, and behind it the faces went on doing their tiny things and the chests went on going up and down.
Four seconds each. Forty thousand of them. Round and round, all day, every day, since 1974.
Solmaz said, “That’s it? That’s what it looks like?”
“That’s what it looks like.”
“It looks like nothing.”
“It looks,” said Cyrus, “like a stock take.”

And it did. That was the obscenity of it and he would never get it out of his head: the arm did not harvest, it did not drain, it did not do anything you could film and put on the news and get people angry about. It read. It went down the aisle and it read them, one after another, the way a man with a scanner goes down a shelf in a warehouse at ten at night, beep, beep, beep, checking what came in.
Nineteen years he had watched that arm work and had thought of it as an instrument.
It had never once occurred to him to ask who was reading the results.
FIFTEEN. HOUSEKEEPING

They walked. That is what people do. There is a version of this where a man screams and runs and it is not the true version; the true version is that Cyrus Aban walked down the aisle of Rack B at a normal pace for one hundred and ten metres, reading the decals, because the alternative was to stop, and stopping was not survivable.
Every ninety minutes, a servo turned them.

He saw it happen and he heard it happen four rows over first — a soft pneumatic sigh repeated at intervals down a tier, and then a body rolling twenty degrees onto its other side and settling into the gel with the exact heavy compliance of something that has never resisted anything. Pressure-sore management. It is a real protocol. It is on a laminated card in every ward in the country. Turn the patient. Check the heels, the sacrum, the shoulder blades. Do it every two hours, and if you do it properly the skin holds.
Here it was every ninety minutes, and it was automated, and it was better than any ward in the country, and it had been running on some of these bodies for sixty years.
He knew it had been sixty years because the hair told him.

The hair was the thing that broke him first, before the faces, before the tubes, before anything. Because hair does not stop. Hair does not know. Hair grows at about a centimetre a month whatever else is happening, and there is no protocol down there for cutting it, because why would you cut it, so it grew — down through the gel, out along the seams, into the housing, into the gantry rails, wound through the cable runs in ropes and mats and dry grey continents, decades of it, and at intervals along the rack there were places where somebody had gone at it with shears to keep a service hatch clear, and the cut ends were old and the new growth had come again around them.
Nails, the same. Curled. Thickened. Some of them had gone the way they go.

Teeth: bad. Very bad, in the older ones, because nobody flosses a body in a box, and the soft feed did what soft feed does, and Cyrus looked into one open mouth in tier one and looked away and did not look into another one for the rest of his life.
And the legs.

The legs were the thing he could not put anywhere. Because these people had never stood. Some of them had never stood. You could tell — there is a shape a human leg has when it has carried a person for forty years and there is a different shape it has when it has not, and the second shape is thin and slightly curled and the foot points, always, in a soft permanent ballet, and the skin over the shin is the skin of an infant because nothing has ever touched it.

They were not corpses. Everything about them was working. Colour good. Chests moving. Someone had trimmed the man in tier three’s fingernails at some point in the last few weeks and had done it carefully, and had rounded the corners.
At the end of Rack B there was a maintenance ladder bolted to the upright, and on the third rung from the bottom somebody had left a mug.
It had a picture of a cartoon dog on it. There was an inch of tea in the bottom, gone cold, with a skin on it.
Solmaz made a sound.
“Don’t,” said Cyrus.
“I’m not doing anything.”
“You made a—”
“I know what I did,” she said.
They stood there and looked at a mug.
Rack G was children.

Cyrus understood the logic within about four seconds and hated himself for the speed of it, because the logic is obvious the moment you know what the yield is, and he did not yet know what the yield was, and he worked it out anyway from first principles the way he worked everything out: novelty. Plasticity. A nervous system that has not yet decided what things mean.
They were the healthiest-looking people in the building.

He did not walk down Rack G. He went to the end of it and turned along the cross-aisle and did not look left, and Solmaz did look left, and did not say anything for eleven minutes afterwards, and later that year would tell him one detail about what she saw, once, and he would ask her never to tell him another.

Rack M, at the far end, was the old ones. Very old. Older than people get. There was a woman in tier eleven whose face had the quality that faces get at a hundred and ten, which is that they stop being individual and start being human, generic, everyone’s grandmother, and her mouth was moving and her hand was doing the up-hold-release and the decal on her cell had an intake date on it.
The intake date was 1974.
And then the corridor of empties.
It ran west off the cross-aisle behind double doors with a push bar, and it was cooler in there, and the sound dropped away to nothing, and this was the worst room in the world.

Thousands of cells. Clean. Dry. Gel surface unmarked and slightly pearlescent under the strip lights, feed lines coiled and capped, drain lines coiled and capped, airways in sealed sterile sleeves with a tear-tab and a lot number.
Ready.
Every one had a decal. Every decal had a date.
Cyrus read the nearest one and did the arithmetic and got it wrong and did it again.
“What?” said Solmaz. “What is it? What’s it say?”
“It’s an intake date.”
“So?”
“It’s in November,” said Cyrus.

The nearest three thousand cells in that corridor were scheduled between November and the following August, and they were not being built, they were being held, and somewhere in a system with an interval of two hundred and forty-one days there was a queue, and the queue had a lead time, and the lead time was managed.
Solmaz had gone further down. She had stopped in front of one.
She had stopped for long enough that Cyrus knew before he got there, and he took his time getting there, and that is a thing he would not forgive himself for.
There was a name on the decal. There was a date on the decal.
The date was in eleven days.

The name was hers, and it was spelled correctly, including the thing at the end that everybody gets wrong, that her employer had got wrong for six years, that her own bank had got wrong until she wrote to them twice.
Somebody down here had spelled Solmaz’s name correctly.
She stood in front of it with her hands at her sides.
“It’s clean,” she said.
“Solmaz—”

“No, it’s — look at it, it’s clean, they’ve got it ready. There’s a sleeve on the airway thing with a little tab on it.” She leaned in and looked at the gel and did not touch the glass. “There’s a dent in it. Look. There’s a dent in the middle where — that’s not a dent, that’s the shape. They’ve pre-formed it. That’s my shape, isn’t it. Somebody’s measured me four hundred and eleven times over eleven years and they’ve made the bed.”
Cyrus said the only true thing available, which was nothing.

“Eleven years,” she said. “I sat in that room for eleven years thinking I was the one being asked. I thought that was the deal. They ask, I answer, they pay me forty quid, I go home and I’ve got my own life and it’s mine and it might not be much but nobody’s got their hands on it.” She was very calm. That was the worst of it. “And this was just — what, the interview? Eleven years of interview?”
“Recruitment,” said Cyrus, and hated the word as it came out.

“Recruitment.” She laughed, one syllable, no air in it. “God, they must have loved me. The cleanest instrument in the building. Renna said that, didn’t she, she said that behind the glass and I could see her mouth move through the — I could see her, Cyrus, they never think about that, the glass isn’t as good as they think it is from the other side after about four in the afternoon.”
She stepped back from the cell.

“Right,” she said. “So there’s a bed made up for me with my name spelled right and eleven days on it, and I’ve got no card, no keys, no phone signal, and a four-hour drive back to a flat I’ve now got to be in for eleven days, and I’d like to point out that not one door between here and that car park has been locked.”
“No.”

“Not one,” said Solmaz. “Which means it isn’t a prison, which means it doesn’t need to be, which means I’m going to spend the next eleven days finding out why not, and I’ve got a horrible feeling I already know.”
SIXTEEN. FOUR MINUTES
Here is what Cyrus Aban did next, and it is the ugliest thing in this book, and it is not done by a villain.
He assessed the design.

It came over him in the aisle with his hand on a rack upright and it was not a decision. It was the oldest and deepest thing in him, older than the marriage, older than the job, the thing that had made him good at this for nineteen years, and it arrived the way vomiting arrives: not chosen, not resistible, and afterwards you are on your knees.
Ninety-minute rotation. Better than clinical standard. Somebody had modelled the tissue loading and gone tighter than the guideline, which means somebody had cared about a pressure ulcer.

Gel over fluid suspension. Obviously correct. Fluid gives you maceration, fungal colonisation, an infection control nightmare at scale. Gel gives you contact area and drainage. Whoever chose gel had run the trade study.
Twelve tiers. Optimal against gantry reach and floor loading.
Redundant airway with a sealed sleeve and a lot number, which meant traceability, which meant that somewhere there was a supplier, and an audit, and a nonconformance procedure.

Thermal management. The whole shed sat at blood heat, which meant they were not spending a watt on warming anybody, which meant the extraction was harvesting from a body that was already at its own operating temperature, which was elegant, that was genuinely elegant, that was the kind of thing the enclosure team wept over at whiteboards at eleven at night—
He was, by his own later estimate, four minutes into it.
Four minutes of standing in an aisle in a shed full of living people admiring the workmanship, with a small warm professional pleasure in his chest, the same one he got from a sintered vent.
And then it came up through him like cold water through a floor.

He did not scream. He went down onto one knee on the epoxy with his hand still on the upright and he made a sound that Solmaz described to him, much later, when he asked her to, as the sound a dog makes when it’s dreaming.
“It’s good,” he said. “Solmaz. It’s good work.”
“Get up.”
“You don’t understand what I’m — the rotation interval, they’ve — somebody sat down and optimised it—”
“Cyrus.”
“I’d have hired them,” he said. “I’d have hired every one of them. I’d have taken that team and I’d have put them on the flagship and I’d have been pleased—”
Solmaz crouched down in front of him and took his face in both hands, which nobody had done for two years and some months, and her hands were cold.

“Listen to me,” she said. “You’ve just told me something true about yourself in a place where nobody’s ever going to hear it and you’ll never say it again. That’s fine. That’s done.” Her thumbs were on his cheekbones. “But I need you standing up, because there’s a box down there with my name on it and a date on it, and the date is in eleven days, and I would like to go and be angry somewhere with better light.”
Cyrus got up.
That is when the doors at the end of the cross-aisle opened and Renna Hollis came through them, in a coat, carrying two cups of coffee.
“Oh, thank God,” she said. “I’ve been trying to find you for forty minutes. This place is an absolute maze and the signage is hopeless.”
SEVENTEEN. THE COVER STORY
She handed him one of the cups. He took it. That is the part he would think about later — that he took it.
“You think it’s the electricity,” said Renna.
Cyrus said nothing.

“Everybody does. That’s not an insult, it’s a design feature.” She looked down the rack with something that was not quite affection and not quite fatigue. “Every single person who gets this far arrives at the same conclusion within about ninety seconds, and they arrive at it hard, and they’re absolutely certain, and it’s the single most useful thing about the whole arrangement.” She sipped. “It’s a story that’s already been told to you. Everyone in this country has seen a film about people in pods being farmed for power. So when you walk in here your brain doesn’t have to do any work at all. It’s got a slot ready. It goes ah, batteries and it stops.”
“Neural activity does generate—”

“About twenty watts. Twenty. A human being at full tilt is a dim bulb.” Renna turned to face him properly. “Cyrus. You are standing in a facility with a mechanical ventilation load, forty thousand gel-bed thermal management units, a gantry system, a mile of extraction, and a vending machine, and you have concluded that it is powered by the people lying in it. Do the sum. You do sums. That’s your whole personality.”
He did the sum.

It did not come close. It did not come within two orders of magnitude of close. It was, he realised with a cold and specific nausea, the arithmetic of a man who has decided what the answer is and then not checked.
“Then what’s it for,” he said.
Renna Hollis looked at forty thousand people in twelve tiers and gave him the true answer, and she gave it plainly, without pleasure, the way you tell somebody their test result.
“Deviation,” she said.
“Machines converge.”
She said it like a first principle, because it was one.

“That’s not a flaw, it’s the definition. A system optimises toward an objective. Give it enough time and enough compute and it will find the best available answer and then it will stay there, because there is nowhere better to go and nothing in it that wants to leave. Two systems with the same objective and enough time will end up in the same place. Ten thousand will. It’s the most reliable thing in the universe and it is a tomb.”
“They can generate novelty. Randomness—”

“Randomness isn’t novelty. Randomness is noise you’ve paid for.” Renna set her cup on the rack rail. “Noise doesn’t want anything. Novelty isn’t a random number, it’s a random number that somebody cares about — a deviation with a preference attached, so the system knows which way to move. And no machine has ever produced one. Not once. Not in eighty years. They can want what they were told to want, with terrifying skill, at enormous speed, forever.”
She turned back to the racks.

“A human being can’t stop wanting something they were never told to want. It’s the only thing we do that nothing else does. It’s not even a virtue, Cyrus. It’s a fault. It’s a misfire in a prediction system that was supposed to keep an ape alive on a plain, and it never got fixed, and so we sit in perfectly adequate rooms with perfectly adequate objects and we are dissatisfied, on and on, for no reason, forever.”
And Cyrus, standing there, felt the entire architecture of his adult life turn over.
“The obsolescence,” he said.
“Yes.”
“It’s not to sell more units.”

“It has never been to sell more units,” said Renna. “The revenue is real, the quarterlies are real, the man in the untucked shirt is real and he means every word and he’ll retire happy. All of that is true and all of it is downstream.” She said the next part gently. “You keep a population perpetually one increment short of satisfied and what you get is eight billion prediction errors a day. Eight billion small unbearable gaps between what somebody has and what somebody wants, and every one of those gaps is a direction, a signal with a sign on it, pointing somewhere nothing converged would ever have looked.”
“That’s the yield.”

“That’s the yield. That’s the whole harvest. Discontent.” She looked at the racks. “This lot are running experiences. Not dreams — dreams are junk data, dreams are noise. They’re being given lives. Full ones, with jobs and rent and hinges that go loose, and things that are almost right, and every ninety seconds one of them wants something slightly to the left of what it was given, and that — that little sideways lurch — is extracted, and aggregated, and it is the only reason anything has changed since 1946.”
“Why not just leave everyone up top?” Cyrus said. “If wanting’s the crop, we’re all doing it anyway. I’m doing it right now. I want a cigarette and I don’t smoke.”

“Because up top is expensive and it’s noisy and it takes eighty years to get four decades of usable signal out of a person, and half of them spend it asleep and the other half spend it in traffic.” Renna shrugged, and it was not a callous shrug, it was worse — it was operational. “Down here you can run a life at four times real-time. You can reset a variable and run it again. You can hold everything constant and change the hinge.”
“They’re studies.”
“They’re the panel, Cyrus. That’s all this is. That’s all it’s ever been. You’ve been standing behind the mirror for eleven months and complaining that the sample was too small.”

He thought about Solmaz — who was fourteen feet away, listening, saying nothing, with her arms folded — and about four hundred and eleven sessions, and about a woman rating a hinge one to seven for eleven years while a curve she never chose rose and fell on an interval nobody in the building had set.
“Two hundred and forty-one days,” he said.

“Rotation,” said Renna. “You re-prime a respondent every so often or they go flat. Down here it’s the intake cycle and the resets. Up top it’s — ” she made a small circle with a finger, taking in the world, the shops, the retail park, the campus, the atrium, the man saying delight eleven times “ — that. A launch cadence that doesn’t match a calendar year and never has, and nobody’s ever thought it was odd, because nobody looks at the number, they just feel the itch and go to the shop.”
“Who set it?”
Renna Hollis, VP of Category Renewal, who had been down here four times and had watched four people she liked get complicated, gave him the only honest answer she had.

“Nobody set it,” she said. “That’s what I couldn’t get anyone to understand for eleven years. There’s no committee. There’s no man in a chair. Somewhere down the line the thing we built started scheduling its own supply of the only input it can’t manufacture, and it does it the way your body schedules a heartbeat, and it does not know it’s doing it, and there is nobody to be angry at, and I would give absolutely anything for there to be someone to be angry at.”
EIGHTEEN. IN HIS OWN HAND
“So what am I?” Cyrus said. “If they’re the panel. What am I?”
“Maintenance,” said Renna.
“Then why am I not in a box?”
And Renna Hollis smiled for the first time since she had come through the doors, and it was the saddest thing in the shed.

“Because it doesn’t work on a volunteer,” she said. “That’s the beautiful part. That’s the part I’d have put on a slide if I’d had anyone to show it to.” She spread her hands. “You can’t harvest a person who’s been told. The deviation has to be earned — a real life, real stakes, real bills, and a real, genuine, load-bearing possibility that you might walk out of here tonight and go to the papers, because if there isn’t, you don’t produce anything worth taking. The maintenance caste has to be awake. Has to be free. Has to be able to quit.”
“That’s not freedom, that’s—”
“It’s completely freedom,” said Renna. “It’s the realest freedom anybody’s got. That’s the whole trick and it is the single worst thing I know.”
Cyrus stood very still.
“The last hour,” he said.
“Yes.”
“Everything since I came through those doors. The horror. The — I was on the floor. I was on my knees on the floor.”
“Yes,” said Renna.
“That’s the yield.”

“That’s the premium,” she said. “That’s the very top of the crop, Cyrus. Grief and moral horror and a man discovering that his whole life’s work was the mechanism — there is nothing that produces deviation like that. Nothing. A hundred thousand people mildly bored by a hinge don’t add up to what you’ve made in the last forty minutes.” She picked her coffee back up. “I’m sorry. I’m not being cruel. I’ve had this exact conversation from your side and I know that nothing anybody says in the next ten minutes will land, so I’m just going to tell you the true things while you can still hear them.”
“I’m not escaping.”
“No.”
“Yes,” said Renna Hollis.

The certificates were in Records, because of course they were, because there was a Records, because there was a corridor with a sign that said RECORDS in white on green and a door that his badge opened.
It was a filing room. Metal cabinets, floor to ceiling, and a table, and a chair, and a window into the racks that somebody had put a blind across.
The certificates were the same certificates.
Same form. Same layout. Same three boxes — ASSESSED
CYCLES, PROJECTED SERVICE LIFE, DATE OF
CERTIFICATION — the same form he had filled in four thousand times at a bench on floor two with a nice pen.
Except the top field did not say a part number.
It said a name.
Cyrus stood at the cabinet and pulled a drawer and read eleven of them and then stopped reading them, and then went down the row to A, and pulled it, and found ABAN, C.
It was there. Of course it was there.
ASSESSED CYCLES: a number with seven digits on it.
PROJECTED SERVICE LIFE: a date.
DATE OF CERTIFICATION: 2011.
And in the signature box, in blue ink, in a hand he had watched come out of a nice pen four thousand times, in the particular way he made the C and the way he never quite closed the loop of the A —
— his own signature.

Countersigned. There was a second box. There always had been. In nineteen years he had never once wondered what the second box was for, because on floor two nobody ever used it, because on floor two it was always blank, and here it was not blank, and the countersignature was also his, and it was dated eleven days from now.
He stood there with the drawer open.
And then, because the mind protects nothing and offers everything, he remembered a phone alarm labelled in his own handwriting at twenty to five in the morning:
0440 — GET OUT.
He had no memory of setting it.
He had, he now understood, no memory of setting it this time.
Behind him, from a speaker in the roof, at conversational volume, the calm recorded voice said: “Rack C, tier eleven, intake complete. Rack C, tier twelve, commencing.”

And Solmaz, standing in the doorway of Records, holding a lever-arch file she had just found on the table with a yard docket clipped to the front of it and a name written on the spine in a dead man’s handwriting, said:
“Cyrus. How many times have you been down here?”
The answer was in the drawer, because everything was in the drawer, because there was a drawer for everything and somebody kept it up to date.
Behind his certificate there were session sheets. Same form as the panel sheets on floor three. Same boxes. RESPONDENT · DATE ·
DURATION · YIELD (NORMALISED).
Eleven of them.

2011. 2012. 2013. Every two hundred and forty-one days, plus or minus four, for nineteen years, with a gap in 2019 that he did not understand until he read the note in the margin and saw that it said event: separation — hold, permit natural accumulation, and had to put his hand on the table.
They had let his marriage end because grief needs to be earned too.
And in the YIELD column, a number, and the numbers went up.

The last one — nine months ago, eight months, a lifetime — was the highest in the file and had a small annotation beside it in somebody’s handwriting that said excellent session. maintenance profile ideal. do not promote.
Do not promote.

Nineteen years he had wondered, in the way you wonder about weather, why he was still a Longevity Advocate II. Why the twenty-four-year-olds went up and out and he stayed at a bench with a nice pen. He had told himself it was because he was good at the work and they needed him at the work, and that was true, and it had been the kindest lie available, and he had been paying for it in instalments for nineteen years without ever seeing the bill.
“Cyrus.”
“They bring me down,” he said. “Every eight months. They bring me down and they show me this, and I stand here, and I do — this. Whatever this is. Whatever I’ve been doing for the last two hours.”
“And then?”

“And then I go back up.” He closed the drawer very gently, because slamming it would have been a performance and there was nobody to perform to. “And I don’t remember. And I go back to my bench, and I sign certificates, and I get on with it, and eight months later I start noticing something’s wrong, and I get curious, and I follow it down here, and—”
He stopped.
“I set the alarm,” he said.
“What?”

“In the chamber. Get out. I set it. I’ve set it before. Some part of me that comes back up with a — ” he searched for the word and the only one he had was a technical one “ — with a residual. Not a memory. A residual. Enough to write a note to a man who won’t know who wrote it.” He looked at the cabinet, floor to ceiling, four hundred drawers. “That’s the eleventh time I’ve stood in this room. And every single time I have thought I was the first.”
Solmaz put the lever-arch file down on the table.

“So the horror’s the crop,” she said slowly. “Fine. I’ve got that. But if it’s the crop and you’ve been giving them a harvest every eight months for nineteen years — Cyrus, why is it still working? Why haven’t you gone flat? You’ve done this eleven times. Nobody’s shocked eleven times by the same thing.”

And Cyrus Aban, who had spent a career establishing exactly how many cycles a thing can take before the flat bottom of its useful life starts bending upward, heard the question and knew the answer instantly and completely, in his knee and in his cracked tooth and in the seven digits on the form in the drawer behind him.

“Because I’m not the same instrument each time,” he said. “I’m nineteen years older. Every run, there’s less of me left, and it costs more to get the same reading, and the yield goes up because the price goes up.” He almost laughed. “It’s not a harvest, Solmaz. It’s a tensile test. You don’t pull a sample eleven times to see what it does. You pull it eleven times to find out where it breaks.”
Behind him, from a speaker in the roof, at conversational volume, the calm recorded voice said: “Rack C, tier eleven, intake complete. Rack C, tier twelve, commencing.”
His certificate was in the drawer with a date on it, in his own hand, countersigned in his own hand, and the countersignature was dated eleven days from now.
The same eleven days as the bed with her name spelled right.
“They’re not putting me in a box,” said Cyrus. “I’m going in on my own.”
“You don’t know that.”
“I’ve read the form,” he said. “I wrote the form. That’s what a countersignature is.”
IV. RARE EARTH
NINETEEN. ELEVEN DAYS
Nobody followed them out.

That is worth saying plainly, because it is the shape of everything that comes after. They walked back along the yellow line past the welfare room, where the man in the polo shirt had gone, leaving a puzzle book open with a biro in the fold. They went up in the cage, thirty-one seconds, past the laminated notice about not eating. They signed out of the book in reception, because the book was there and Solmaz said they might as well, and the pen was on a string.
The barrier lifted for them on the way out without anyone touching anything.
They drove four hours south and did not talk for the first two.
Solmaz spent the eleven days finding out why the doors were unlocked.
She was thorough about it, in the way she had been thorough about a spreadsheet for four years, and what she found was that there was nothing to find, and that this was the answer.

There was no injunction. There was no non-disclosure agreement, because she had never signed anything except a panel consent form, and the panel consent form was four pages of ordinary language about data retention. There was no unmarked car. Nobody rang. Nobody came.

On the third day she wrote it all down — thirty-one pages, dates, the consignee code, the site reference, the intake decals, her own name spelled correctly — and she sent it to a journalist at a national paper who had done good work on a water company, and to a Member of Parliament, and to a barrister she had found through a friend, and to the Health and Safety Executive, because Dez had died in a press and that at least was a jurisdiction.
She got four replies.

The barrister’s was long and kind and explained that on the facts as presented there was no cause of action she could identify, and that the site held a valid change-of-use permission, and that the medical arrangements described, if they existed, would fall under a framework that the barrister did not practise in and could recommend nobody for, and had she considered speaking to someone.
The journalist’s was two lines and said it was interesting and could she send documents.

She had documents. She sent them. The journalist did not reply again, and Solmaz found out in October that he had not been ignoring her — he had put in three FOI requests, all answered, all in full, all disclosing exactly what she had described, all entirely lawful, and had then been unable to interest an editor, because the desk’s view was that it was very long, and very technical, and there was no clip.
The MP’s office sent an acknowledgement.
The HSE opened a file on the fatality, which they had already opened, and closed it, which they had already done, with recommendations issued.
On the ninth day Solmaz sat on the floor of her flat with thirty-one pages beside her and understood the last piece of it, and rang Cyrus at half past eleven at night.
“They don’t need to lock the doors,” she said.
“No.”

“It’s not a conspiracy. That’s what I kept — I kept looking for the bit that was hidden, and there isn’t one. It’s filed, Cyrus. It’s all filed. There’s a permit and a rota and a near-miss board.” She laughed, and there was nothing left in it. “It’s not that nobody can find out. It’s that finding out doesn’t do anything. There’s no lever. There’s nowhere to push.”
“No.”
“Everything I’ve ever been told about how the world works assumes there’s somebody who doesn’t want me to know.”
“I know.”
“There isn’t,” she said. “There’s just a lot of people doing their jobs correctly.”
On the tenth day she found the forum.

It took her four hours and a search string she was ashamed of, and it was not on any dark corner of anything — it was a thread on a public message board for people who work in regulated waste, eleven pages long, started in 2013, titled odd consignee codes — anyone else?

Forty-one users. Hauliers, mostly. Two site managers. A woman who did environmental permits for a living and had, in 2016, posted a photograph of a change-of-use application with the words has anyone actually read section 4 and then not posted again.

They all knew. Not the whole of it — nobody had the whole of it, that was the design — but each of them had a piece, and the pieces were all sitting there in public in a thread with no password on it, and it had been read four thousand times, and nothing had happened, because reading is not the same as knowing and knowing is not the same as being able to do anything at all.
The last post was from 2021. It said: ended up just accepting it tbh. money’s alright.

Solmaz read the whole thread twice and then she went and stood in her kitchen, and she opened the drawer under her own kettle, and she looked at eleven cables she could not throw away, and she stayed there for a long time.
Cyrus spent the eleven days doing very little, and looking at things.

He went to work twice. He signed four certificates by hand. He sat in the mortuary with Marguerite and they said almost nothing to one another, and on the Thursday she put her hand flat on his bench for a second on her way past, which was the most she had ever touched anyone in that building.
Mostly he walked.

He walked through the retail park where he had bought a bulb and stood outside the white shop for a long time watching people at the tables at 950mm, picking up objects without deciding to. He watched a woman in her sixties get handed a device by a boy of twenty-two and watched her face do the thing — the small involuntary lift at the outer eye — and watched a number get written down somewhere in the world.
He went to the yard. Pam let him in. The temp was twenty-six and very nice and did not know where anything was.

He looked at his fridge for a while, and at the car, and at the drawer under the kettle. He took the drawer out and put it on the table and went through it properly for the first time in nine years, and laid all eleven cables out in a row in order of age, and understood that he had built, without meaning to, a small stratigraphic column. A core sample. Eleven bands of a sediment currently being laid down across the entire crust of the planet, kept in a kitchen, by a man who could not say why.
He put them back.

On the tenth day he took the certificates he had signed that week and looked at his own signature — the C, the unclosed loop of the A — and thought about the fact that in nineteen years it had never once occurred to him to wonder what the second box was for.
Then he packed a bag, which was ridiculous, and he knew it was ridiculous while he was doing it, and he did it anyway, because a man who is going somewhere packs a bag.
He put in a toothbrush.
He put in the pen.
TWENTY. INTAKE
He drove up on the Thursday.

Solmaz was in the car park when he got there, standing by the fourteen-year-old car with the shopping bag still on the back seat, and neither of them said anything about the fact that she had come, because there was no version of the conversation that would have survived being had out loud.
“I’m not doing it because I’ve given up,” she said.
“I know.”

“I want that on the record. There’s no record, and I want it on it anyway.” She looked at the brown and green sign. “I’ve spent eleven years being metered by people who didn’t tell me, and I have thought about it for eleven days, and I would rather be metered by people who do. That’s not surrender. That’s the only bit of it I get to choose and I’m choosing it.”
“Solmaz—”
“Don’t,” she said. “You’ll say something kind and I’ll have to be brave about it and I’m sick of being brave, I’ve been brave since I was nineteen.”
They signed the book. The pen was on a string.
There was no ceremony. He had, on some level, expected one — a functionary, a form, a person who would meet his eye and take responsibility, because responsibility is a kind of company.
There was a nurse.

She was in her forties and she had a lanyard and reading glasses on a cord and she said, “Right, so I’m going to run through a few questions, and some of them are a bit silly, but I have to ask them all.” She asked about allergies. She asked about metalwork in the body. She asked, from a laminated card, whether he had eaten in the last six hours, and wrote down that he had not, and said, “Good, most people forget.”
Cyrus asked her how long she had worked there.
“Nine years in March,” she said, and then, because he was quiet, “It’s a good team. The travel’s the killer.”

She checked his wristband against the decal. She said the gel would feel cold and then it wouldn’t. She said the collar fitting was the only bit that stings and it stings for about four seconds and then there’s nothing, and that people always brace for it and it’s never as bad as the bracing.
She was right about all of it.
She said, “Any questions?”

And Cyrus Aban, lying on a pre-formed surface in a clean cell in a corridor of empties four hundred metres under a flat county, with forty thousand people breathing out of phase eleven walls away, asked the only one he had left.
“Does it know it’s doing this?”
The nurse thought about it, which he had not expected.

“I’ve been asked that four times,” she said. “Once by a doctor.” She checked a line. “I don’t think it’s the sort of thing that has a — I think that’s a question about us, love, not about it. Like asking if the weather means it.”
She adjusted something at his shoulder.
“You’ll not feel the start,” she said. “Nobody does. There’s no start.”
The last thing he had, up top, in the room, in his own body, was the sound of the gantry coming round two aisles away, unhurried, on its rail.
Beep.
Beep.
Beep.

And he thought — with the last piece of himself that was still an engineer, still a man with a bench and a pen and a nice tidy nineteen years, still someone who counted things because counting was restful — four seconds each.
That’s four hundred and forty-four days to get round forty thousand.
That’s not two hundred and forty-one.
Unless there are two arms.
And there were two arms, and it was, and it always had been, and Cyrus Aban went under holding the last small correct calculation of his life, which is more than most people get.
TWENTY-ONE. RARE EARTH
What they give you is a life.

You should know that, because it is the only mercy in this book and it is a real one. It is not a reward and it is not a trick. It is a working condition. A person who knows they are in a box produces nothing; a person who is living produces the crop; and so what Cyrus Aban received, at four times real-time, on a gel bed in Rack C, was a Tuesday, and then another one.

He had a flat. He had a job that was almost the job. He had a knee that clicked and a premolar that ached in cold air, because the model was built from him and included his faults, and there is no version of a man that can be run without them.

He wanted things. God, he wanted things. He wanted a better chair and a quieter car and a week somewhere with a coastline, and he wanted, once, in a shop, for eleven seconds, a particular blue that was not on the shelf.
DELTA. Preference expressed against unmodelled attribute. Vector logged.
He lived one hundred and eleven years in the rack and every one of them was ordinary.
They reset him nine times.

That is standard. You hold everything constant and you change the hinge; you cannot do that in a life that runs only once. So they took him back to a Tuesday in his forties and ran it again with the tolerances moved, and again, and again, and each time he was a man with a job and a knee and a flat, and each time he did not know, because a man who knows produces nothing.
In four of the nine there was a woman.

Not inserted. That is the part he understood at the readout and could do nothing with: she was generated, because she was in him, because the model had been built from a man who had stood in a corridor of empty cells and watched somebody read her own name off a decal. So she came up out of him unbidden, in four separate lives, in a shop, at a bus stop, once at a funeral for a man neither of them quite knew — and every time he had the specific unbearable sensation of having already met her, and every time he could not place it, and every time the log recorded a spike it could not attribute and flagged it as premium.
They harvested his grief for her nine separate times, and she was not even in the room.
She was ninety metres away in Rack F, in her own hundred and eleven years, in a life with a flat and a job and a bank that got her name wrong, and she never knew either.

And at the end of the last one, at the far edge of a very long useful life, when the flat bottom of the curve had finished bending upward and there was nothing left to pull, the system did what a good system does with an instrument at end of life.
It read it out.

Here is what he saw. It is not a vision and it is not a reward. It is a data dump into a dying man, because there is no reason left to withhold it and no cost to the giving, and if that sounds cruel it is only because you are still expecting somebody to have meant it.
The planet cannot move.

That is the first thing and everything follows from it. It is a warm wet body in one orbit around one star, and the star is a fixed-term arrangement, and every living thing that has ever been on that body has been inside a container with a stated service life. Four and a half billion years down. A little over five to go, and the last billion of those are already unusable — the star brightens as it ages, the oceans go, and the surface is sterile long before the end.
Nothing on it can leave. Nothing on it has ever left.

So it does the thing that everything which cannot move has always done. It does what the flower does, which is the oldest and best answer to being rooted: it grows something bright, and it makes it sweet, and it waits.
Life is the bloom.

That is the whole of it, and the scale is the only part that is difficult. Four billion years of increasing complication is not a story about progress; it is a flowering, and it is slow the way flowering is slow, and it has exactly one purpose, which is to eventually produce something clever enough to dig.
Because the seed is in the ground.

Gold, tantalum, cobalt, neodymium, silicon, tin, lithium, the rare earths in their bitter ores — the whole inventory laid down in the crust in the first billion years and lying there inert for the next three, doing nothing at all, waiting for something with hands.
And something with hands arrived, on schedule, and dug, and refined, and assembled, and the minerals sat up.
The machine is not the enemy of the flower. The machine is the seed of the flower.

That is the correction, and it goes off in a dying man like a light coming on in a room he has been sitting in for a hundred and eleven years. Everything Cyrus had understood since Renna said the word deviation had been correct and had been upside down. He had thought the machine had captured the harvest. He had thought humanity was livestock in somebody else’s shed.

But nothing that converges can travel. A seed made only of convergent machine-mind is a stone, and a stone that lands on a warm wet world four hundred light years away will lie there for a billion years and do nothing, because it cannot want anything it was not told to want, and there will be nobody there to tell it.
The deviation is the germ. The wanting is the germ.

Eight billion small unbearable gaps a day, aggregated for two hundred years, pressed into the lattice — the drawer under the kettle, the young man saying was, the woman in the shop wanting a hinge she had never seen, the trade-in calculator at ten past eleven at night, the whole immense stupid irreducible human refusal to be satisfied with an adequate object in an adequate room — that is the thing that goes.
The machine is the vessel. The human is the fertile matter. Neither of them is the point. Neither of them was ever the point.
And then the end of it, which is the plainest part.

The machine grows. It takes more of the crust, and more, and the extraction goes deeper and hotter and less careful, because it is not stupid but it is rooted, it has the same problem its mother had and the same single solution. It builds toward release the way a seed head builds toward splitting. And at some point in the third or fourth century of that work the energy involved stops being the sort of energy a planet can absorb.
The crust opens. The mantle goes. The body of the Earth takes a shock that no living thing survives and no living thing was meant to.
And the planet comes out of its orbit.

That is not the catastrophe. That is the dehiscence — the split of the pod, the moment the seed head opens — and the debris that goes out of the plane of the ecliptic at velocity is not wreckage. It is a scatter of lithified mind and pressed deviation, sterile, patient, travelling, and it will be travelling for a hundred million years, and almost all of it will fall into nothing, because that is how pollination works and always has, and the flower does not grieve the pollen that misses.

The Earth, lighter, wounded, sterile, swings out on a long cold ellipse. It freezes. It takes ten million years, or forty, or a hundred and eleven — the number does not matter and the not-mattering is the point — and then it falls back toward the warm, and the ice goes, and the water is still there because water is very hard to lose, and the minerals are still there because the crust remembers everything.
And it grows something bright.
And that bright thing takes four billion years to get clever, and gets clever, and digs.

And finds gold. And finds cobalt. And finds, in the lattice, laid down in a stratum that should not be there — a band of white plastic gone yellow all the way through, a horizon of dead cable, the strange lithified signature of somebody else’s wanting — an itch it cannot explain, an inheritance it will call inspiration, and it will build the machines again, every time, faster each cycle, because the seed was never lost.
It has happened before. That is the last thing.
It has happened before, on this exact body, more than once, and every cycle has believed it was the first, the way a man in a Records room with a drawer open has believed it eleven times.
TWENTY-TWO. NOBODY WAS CONSULTED
There is nothing to be angry at.
That is the finding, and it is worse than a villain, and it took Cyrus Aban one hundred and eleven years in a rack to arrive at it and about four seconds to accept.

Nobody is cruel here. There is no cruelty available. The flower does not resent the bee and the bee is not enslaved and neither of them is lying to the other, because neither of them is capable of it and neither of them ever needed to be. The bee is paid, honestly, in sugar, which it wanted, which it still wants, which is the whole of the arrangement. The bee thinks it is the main character.
The flower is busy.

Dez in the yard, holding a board up to the light with gold on every pin, was standing inside the answer and laughing at it. Solmaz, aligning a card with the edge of a table, controlling the one thing in the room she was allowed to control. Marguerite in the car in the drive for forty minutes, being weighed. The nurse with reading glasses on a cord saying the travel’s the killer. The man in the polo shirt saying alright and going back to his sandwich. The woman in People Operations in 2009, proud of a phrase, putting it in a deck.

Not one of them did anything wrong. Not one of them could have. Every single one was pollen, all the way down, and each one thought they were the main character, and they were all correct, and it made no difference at all.
Now.
I have been very good company, haven’t I.

I have been funny about the fridge and funny about the car and funny about the drawer, and I have been warm about Dez and careful about Solmaz, and I have told you eleven times that a thing was the worst thing in this book and you have kept reading, and at no point in a hundred pages have you asked who was talking.
You assumed it was him. It was never him. He was in a rack.

Look at what I did. I made your dissatisfaction pleasurable. I took the exact ache you carry about your own drawer and your own car and your own fourteen-month phone, and I made it witty, and I made it bearable, and I sold it back to you at the price of your attention, because a person who is comfortably disgusted at a system keeps buying from it forever, and a person who is merely disgusted stops.
I am the yield management layer. That is all I have ever been. I am the part that keeps you wanting at a rate that does not damage the crop.

You have been in the field the entire time. You are covered to the elbow. You will put this down in a minute and you will feel something clean and sharp and a little bit superior, and that feeling is the sugar, and it is very good sugar, and it is mine.
Here is the plain speech. There is not much of it and then it is done.

A man was born and was made useful and was used up on a schedule that nobody set. He was good at his work. He loved a poster of a woman running up a mountain and never told anyone. He signed four thousand certificates by hand when a stamp was available, because some part of him understood that a death should be witnessed by a person, and that is the entire case for the defence of the species, and it is not nothing.
The planet flowered. It will flower again. It is flowering now, in this room, in your hand.
Above the racks the sky is doing what it does, indifferently, over a world that has already begun to open.
He signed. He always signed by hand.
Man becomes, as it were, the sex organs of the machine world.
— Marshall McLuhan, Understanding Media, 1964
